body:
Something I just realized is that this nonlinear scaled emission that I suggested is not mathematically correct when using addition. (e.g. 0.5+0.9=1.4 becomes 0.5+0.9 ~= 3.1.) As a result, overlapping emissive volumes look far too bright. For accurate addition, you'd have to load, unscale, add, rescale, then store. There's no reasonable way this is possible with atomic image operations.

The alternative reduced-bits option is unfortunate because 7 bits per color yields significant color inaccuracy at low fog densities. Setting fog density below 1/127, instead of yellowing, would truncate all emission. This makes thin clouds look terrifying if you ask me.

The only ways around the imprecision problem that I can think of are:
A. Reduce the emission range
B. Add another image3D to provide more bits
C. Add a fog-volume-density linear-scale property to the environment, replacing the current nonlinear scaling. It scales the density/emission before writing and unscales it after reading, just like the nonlinear scaling. This would effectively give the user control over the range of precision.

I think option C is the best one, but that could be done in another PR.

body:
I added another option to the previous comments:

> D. Use emission_energy in the environment to scale all emissive colors and force emission in the shaders to cap at 1 (e.g. we would be defining emission color in the volume and emission energy globally)

Ultimately, I think going with A is probably fine. Density is usually quite low and since Emission scales with Density it will be quite low as well. In cases where both emission and density are high, clamping to 4 should be sufficient (only the emission at the edge of the volume will be seen anyway). The range of 0-8 was arbitrarily chosen, so I don't feel bad changing it. 

If we still notice issues stemming from low precision we can select one of the other options.

body:
From what I can find, the `MONO_GLUE_ENABLED` flag only gets added with `mono_glue=yes`, and it only gets added to the cloned instance of `env` for the mono module, which I don't think I have access to at this point in the script.
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/8f7f5846397297fff6e8a08f89bc60ce658699cc/modules/mono/SCsub#L18

As for the `cli_args` extras, it kind of has to be hardcoded this way because each one of these extra module configs creates variants that only target the default engine with whatever module its being defined for. I couldn't conceive a good way to 'mix and match' modules in a way that would work with VS. If these extra args were to be inferred from the `scons` command that ended up at this point, I don't think there isn't a clean way to determine which scons flag has to be appended to the build args for a given module's variants.

 It kind of sucked that I even had to add the condition that `module_mono_enabled=yes` was given to be able to generate the mono variants. I was hoping that the mono variants could just be generated agnostic of other arguments to scons, but the mono `.cpp` files only got globbed with that flag added.

As for the path thing, it was basically copy/pasted from here:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/ffab3949e365598271e50705e358864eecfb64d8/modules/mono/build_scripts/mono_configure.py#L156

tl;dr My understanding is that the mono-specific configurations that would be useful here get collected somewhere else, being `env_mono` in its SCsub, that can't be accessed here (or that I just don't know how to do it). Since I expect other modules' variants might get added here later, it wouldn't be possible to figure out which config values get added to which variants based solely on the global context.

Also, why the array of 6 possible names? How many architectures are we actually supporting? Are those 6 different architectures or aliases of the same? We only need to support one name, users should use that name.
author: akien-mga

body:
They're aliases, but I can remove them.

> All other architectures are handled in the relevant platforms' `detect.py`, not in the main `SConstruct`.

Are you sure that's the best approach? This code is generally applicable, even if currently the only OS that can use it at the moment is X11 / LinuxBSD. In all cases of ARM support in Godot (Mac, iPhone, Android, UWP) there are OS-specific things in the `detect.py`, but this isn't OS-specific, all it does is tell the compiler to use the architecture.

~~Also, placing this logic here gives us the opportunity to alter the `suffix`. For the current implementation of ARM in `detect.py` it seems that this is done inconsistently. Mac, iPhone, and UWP don't put the architecture in the suffix, while with Android it adds to `extra_suffix`.~~
author: aaronfranke

body:
Architecture and compiler go together, I'm pretty sure `-march=rv64gc` is not supported by MSVC. So it doesn't make sense for Windows or UWP.

If the only OS we aim to support is Linux, then this should go in the Linux `detect.py`.

If eventually we want to add support for more platforms, we can refactor.

For example almost all platforms support 32-bit or 64-bit ARM platforms, but almost none use the same config to target it. Targeting arm64 via the Xcode SDK is not the same as doing it via the Android NDK, or the UWP SDK, or native GCC or Clang for Linux.
author: akien-mga

body:
> Also, placing this logic here gives us the opportunity to alter the `suffix` (and not the `extra_suffix`). For the current implementation of ARM in `detect.py` it seems that this is done inconsistently. Mac, iPhone, and UWP don't put the architecture in the suffix, while with Android it adds to `extra_suffix`.

This all needs a refactor but that's not something that should be started here for RISC-V. See https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/1416.
author: akien-mga

body:
I would move this to the Linux `detect.py` too. It won't add the `arch` to `extra_suffix`, but this isn't done for `i386`, `i686`, `x86_64`, `armv7hl` or` aarch64` on Linux currently, so we shouldn't do it for `rv64` only.

Like it's done for `aarch64` currently, it should be clear to someone compiling on RISC-V hardware that their `godot.linuxbsd.opt.tools.64` binary targets RISC-V (especially if they passed `arch=rv64` for that).
author: akien-mga

body: BTW, this check also makes it impossible to cross-compile from RISC-V to other architectures.
author: akien-mga

body:
I made the change locally to test it. To my surprise, it actually does add the arch to the suffix. It calls the configure method on line 397. So yeah, moving this to `detect.py` works well.

> BTW, this check also makes it impossible to cross-compile from RISC-V to other architectures.

It's not possible to cross-compile for x86 regardless as far as I can tell. For this code specifically, it doesn't make it impossible because this code only runs `if env["arch"] == ""` so you just have to say `arch=arm64` or `arch=x86_64`, even if it's not picked up by the engine, this will stop it from being equal to `""`. Still, as I mentioned it's not possible to cross-compile for x86 regardless, we don't have any code in the build system to tell the compiler to target x86. Also, cross-compiling *from* RISC-V is super niche :P

The method `mono_class_get_element_class` gets the MonoClass of the array's elements so for a `MyEnum[]` array it gets the MonoClass for `MyEnum` and then I get the MonoType with `mono_class_get_type` of the MonoClass I got.

body:
I think I understand what's happening now. The `(MonoArrayType *)` is wrong because that would be supposed to represent `MyEnum[]` in this case.
The reason this is working is because `mono_class_get_type` returns the `MonoType*` representing `MyEnum`. Then you do a C cast which reinterprets it as `MonoArrayType *`. The subsequent accesses to the `eklass` (element class) field work correctly because of the layout of both structs:

https://github.com/mono/mono/blob/8266c5604b8c03882f2b06af27fdea46b142d6b9/mono/metadata/metadata.h#L325-L326
https://github.com/mono/mono/blob/8266c5604b8c03882f2b06af27fdea46b142d6b9/mono/metadata/metadata-internals.h#L24-L26

You're actually accessing the `MonoType::klass` field.

The following:
```cpp
MonoArrayType *array_type = (MonoArrayType *)mono_class_get_type(c);
elem_class = array_type->eklass;
```

Should be:

```cpp
elem_class = mono_class_from_mono_type(elem_type);
```

body:
For the record, just reposting some comments from @RandomShaper and @smix8 after I asked maintainers about how to do this properly.

> @RandomShaper
> `Resource::emit_changed()` can only work from the main thread or a resource loading thread.
> In the latter case, it employs some deferring magic to keep things fine on the main thread.
> It won't handle being called from an arbitrarty thread, which seems to be the case here.
> I'd like to know why it is being called from another thread in the first place.

> @smix8 
> I think the problem in that PR is more that the `CameraServer.add_feed()` function, that should be called on the main thread, is called directly from the thread function that this PR adds. The base CameraServer also emits a changed signals with that function but without any deferred so that entire function is clearly designed to be only called on the main thread.
> Using the call_deferred() is always a sloppy fix, because as the PR maker already noted, you sometimes need to do it twice because something else might flush the queue before while whatever uses your signal connected node or resource might still be locked. It is not running just once each frame.
> imo the CameraServer should just sync its own updates with the main thread from its own queue, piggybacking on the main message queue with signals is always a valley of tears because that queue gets flushed at random points in the physics, scenetree, and main loop and maybe even in some other cursed places as well. It is totally overloaded with ugly hacks by now.

> @RandomShaper
> `SceneTree`'s `process_frame` signal may be a suitable point to hook to.

> @smix8 
> or do as e.g. the XRServer and just sync/process before all the script loop so things are updated before user scripts try to work with it.

This PR has been waiting long enough so I don't think this should be blocking now, but that's some food for thought and maybe further rework of the implementation to avoid future issues.

> This calculation seems only required here if LOD is active for this instance. This could be set efficiently with e.g. a bool when setting the LOD params for the instance. i.e.:

Do we need a dedicated boolean field for this? We can check if LOD is enabled by checking whether the min range *or* max range is greater than 0 (exclusive). We can also check for hysteresis being greater than 0 (exclusive) if any of those conditions is true, but lazy evaluation can take care of that for us anyway.

author: Calinou

body:
I haven't profiled this, but imo a good aim is to make any new code as cheap as possible for instances that aren't using LOD. We essentially should aim not to be doing extra unnecessary calculations for the 99% of times where people aren't using LOD on an instance.

Doing unneeded distance calculations, and checking two float values against `CMP_EPSILON` is not as cheap as just detecting a bool is set to false which will likely be the cheapest conditional (bear in mind on some mobile floating point math could even be emulated). This double float check is additionally now not required at runtime _should the bool be set to true_.

There are lots of occasions where just doing things unoptimized are fine (where code clarity is important, and it isn't performance sensitive), but inside the renderer imo we should strive to make it as efficient as possible as there is a fair amount of churn, and we are just wasting cycles and battery on mobile.

Looking at the `Instance : RasterizerScene::InstanceBase` structure, it looks like `RID lod_instance` is unused so could be removed. You could for instance add a bool up with the `update_materials` bools, and you could possibly make them 1 bit too (e.g. `bool update_aabb : 1;`), so they would likely be no more than 32 bit between them.

In `instance_geometry_set_draw_range()` you could just do something like this:
```
instance->using_lod = (instance->lod_begin > CMP_EPSILON) || (instance->lod_end > CMP_EPSILON);
```
Therefore the float check is done once (rarely) when setting the params, and the cheap bool test can be done at runtime on each frame on each `prepare_scene`.

There's a bug here that can affect projects that choose to use the non-hidden directory. If `res://godot/...` does not exist yet when the client is instantiated, then it will default to `res://.godot/...` (hidden), create that directory and watch for file changes on that one instead of `res://godot/...`.
This won't cause any regressions for projects using the default, which is the hidden directory, so I think the change is still ok for now.
I think it's not ok for the client to create the directory on its own, but `FileSystemWatcher` requires the directory to exist and creating it was the easiest solution. I'll probably change that in the future. It will require listening for each directory creation before listening for the file changes.

What will happen with this change is that the depth buffer will be treated as if it is only 200 units deep (even if it is representing a scene that is 4000 units deep) so to the SSAO objects that are 1000 units apart will look like they are only 50 units apart. body:
```suggestion
const SPEED: float = 5.0
const JUMP_FORCE: float = 4.5
```

* These values are only used in a float context, and it perfectly valid for a user to set a speed of `5.5` etc, so we should make these floats.
* The specific numbers used here are indeed arbitrary, but I am suggesting that they change to these values. I used Minecraft and real life as a reference.
  * For speed, the Minecraft wiki says "Sprinting allows the player to move at around 5.612 meters/second, which is 30 percent faster than the normal walking speed of around 4.317 m/s", so 5 is right in-between those values. The first Google result for running speed says "The average human running speed in m/s is typically 5 meters per second", which sounds about right to me. Aside from that, it subjectively feels too fast at 8.0 m/s from my own experience with games. Also, even at 5.0, this is over 3 and a half times average walking speed.
  * The jump force of 4.5 allows jumping up one meter (one block in Minecraft). This is a large value compared to real life, but I think that this amount of jumping would generally be expected in games, so this is a good default value IMO.
  * Feel free to disagree with me on this if you have a specific reason in mind.

I suggest doing it the same as in ``renderer_canvas_render_rd`` as described in this comment https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/51957#issuecomment-924192168

body:
```suggestion
	 /* Animation compression page format (version 1):
	 *
	 * Animation uses bitwidth based compression separated into small pages. The intention is that pages fit easily in the cache, so decoding is cache efficient.
	 * The page-based nature also makes future animation streaming from disk possible.
	 *
	 * Actual format:
	 *
	 * num_compressed_tracks = bounds.size()
	 * header : (x num_compressed_tracks)
	 * -------
	 * timeline_keys_offset : uint32_t - offset to time keys
	 * timeline_size : uint32_t - amount of time keys
	 * data_keys_offset : uint32_t offset to key data
	 *
	 * time key (uint32_t):
	 * ------------------
	 * frame : bits 0-15 - time offset of key, computed as: page.time_offset + frame * (1.0/fps)
	 * data_key_offset : bits 16-27 - offset to key data, computed as: data_keys_offset * 4 + data_key_offset
	 * data_key_count : bits 28-31 - amount of data keys pointed to, computed as: data_key_count+1 (max 16)
	 *
	 * data key:
	 * ---------
	 * X / Blend Shape : uint16_t - X coordinate of XYZ vector key, or Blend Shape value. If Blend shape, Y and Z are not present and can be ignored.
	 * Y : uint16_t
	 * Z : uint16_t
	 * If data_key_count+1 > 1 (if more than 1 key is stored):
	 * data_bitwidth : uint16_t - This is only present if data_key_count > 1. Contains delta bitwidth information.
	 *    X / Blend Shape delta bitwidth: bits 0-3 - 
	 	 * if 0, nothing is present for X (use the first key-value for subsequent keys), 
        	 * else assume the number of bits present for each element (+ 1 for sign). Assumed always 16 bits, delta max signed 15 bits, with underflow and overflow supported.
	 *    Y delta bitwidth : bits 4-7
	 *    Z delta bitwidth : bits 8-11
	 *    FRAME delta bitwidth : 12-15 bits - always present (obviously), actual bitwidth is FRAME+1
	 * Data key is 4 bytes long for Blend Shapes, 8 bytes long for pos/rot/scale.
	 *
	 * delta keys:
	 * -----------
	 * Compressed format is packed in the following format after the data key, containing delta keys one after the next in a tightly bit packed fashion.
	 * FRAME bits -> X / Blend Shape Bits (if bitwidth > 0) -> Y Bits (if not Blend Shape and Y Bitwidth > 0) -> Z Bits (if not Blend Shape and Z Bitwidth > 0)
	 *
	 * data key format:
	 * ----------------
	 * Decoding keys means starting from the base key and going key by key applying deltas until the proper position is reached needed for interpolation.
	 * Resulting values are uint32_t
	 * data for X / Blend Shape, Y and Z must be normalized first: unorm = float(data) / 65535.0
	 * **Blend Shape**: (unorm * 2.0 - 1.0) * Compression::BLEND_SHAPE_RANGE
	 * **Pos/Scale**: unorm_vec3 * bounds[track].size + bounds[track].position
	 * **Rotation**: Quaternion(Vector3::octahedron_decode(unorm_vec3.xy),unorm_vec3.z * Math_PI * 2.0)
	 * **Frame**: page.time_offset + frame * (1.0/fps)
	 */
```

body:
The reason is simply that prefixed `++` is more performant. Postfixed `++` generates a temporary variable on the stack which in this case is probably optimized out by the compiler given that `sign` is a primitive type. Over non-primitive types, postfixed `++` may not be optimized by the compiler automatically due to the complexity involved over constructors and/or memory allocators.

I tend to prioritize performance over code style and readability, but that being said I'm going to drop this change. It's simply a change I dragged from salvaging #52524. I'll push performance issues out of the scope for this PR.

author: akien-mga

body:
In this code the user is modifying a key within a method-type track of an `Animation`, right? The number of arguments for a method-type track in an `Animation` is bound by the maximum number of arguments the `AnimationPlayer` itself supports when playing this track. `VARIANT_ARG_MAX` is related. I fail to see how it could not.  Keep an eye on `Animation::TYPE_METHOD`.

When the AnimationPlayer attempts to play the method-type track, it will run the following code (only pay attention to the first line, the last line, and `params` near the bottom):
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/b197de6f5f1e61a9cecf0a29aadea0fb024b1edf/scene/animation/animation_player.cpp#L527-L548

The very last line of that code block has a direct reference to `VARIANT_ARG_MAX`. That check is there because further below `AnimationPlayer` reconstructs the method call extracted from the track:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/b197de6f5f1e61a9cecf0a29aadea0fb024b1edf/scene/animation/animation_player.cpp#L556-L573
The `params` array holds the number of arguments previously saved on the track through the `AnimationTrackEditor`. Everytime `VARIANT_ARG_MAX` is updated, that last code block needs to be updated to support the maximum number of arguments.

body:
Yes, to properly fix https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/46100 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/46101 (beyond #59760) would require separating out the mouse double-clicks from the double-taps. So that the start of the second tap is not also detected as the start of a second single click.
Note: The main challenge is ensuring the release of the second click releases the double tap too.
author: madmiraal

body:
>  So that the start of the second tap is not also detected as the start of a second single click.

@madmiraal  That's part of a larger issue that also affects other gestures besides double-taps. Our current input logic sends both the raw input events (down, move, up) and the processed input events (detected gestures) to the native layer, so in scenarios where a gesture is detected, we end double-counting.

We need to update the logic so that we only sends raw input events when a gesture is not detected; it's part of a larger fix I'll be looking at unless one of you is up to the task :)

For this issue, we can scope the fix to re-enabling finger double-taps using the proposal I highlighted above since at the moment they're disabled because of the button mask value.
On top of fixing finger double-taps, this will allow to leverage the current logic which provide information regarding the source of the event when it's not a finger.

body: In Godot generally classes are either PODs or full fledged, and in this case `Operation` will not clearly be either of those. This technique is discouraged to be used every frame, as these string methods are not efficient.

If you look in the comment section at the top of `project_settings.h`, there are now two methods to only query this when project settings have changed.

From `VisualServerScene`, as it cannot receive signals, you probably want to cache this value, and call `ProjectSettings::has_changes()` and only call GLOBAL_GET if changes have occurred.

We can probably centralize this for all such project settings that need to be cached in e.g. `VisualServer`. If you are not sure how to do this, just remind me after such a change and I can put this in.

We may alternatively be able to use a little macro to do this and store the cached value in a static, much like the `WARN_PRINT_ONCE` type macros.

I see here the bigges problem with this approach.

In Godot we're not using exceptions (some 3rd-party code may be, but Godot's own codebase isn't), so `try/catch` is forbidden. However, let's consider for a moment if the use case here is strong enough. If I'm not mistaken, what you are attempting to catch here is a segfault (i.e., accessing memory no longer owned by the process), being that a way to detect that an `RID` is dangling. But wouldn't it be possible that a future `RID` data ends up being alocated at the same (or overlapping) memory address, rendering that sort of check useless?

That's a bit like the dangling `Variant` issue we use to have.

body:
Using `rest_info()` is not actually giving the results you're expecting. It's meant for contact detection and gives you the deepest collision point, so depending on the motion length and shape size you can get different results, not necessarily the nearest collision along the path.

Unfortunately there's currently no good API that gives you all the information you need for all collisions.

What I would suggest for now is:

- You can keep using `cast_motion()` for the safe/unsafe distances, and later the physics server API can be improved to provide more information along with it, so you will be able to get more details about the closest collision.

- For the multiple collision results, you can call `intersect_shape()` just once instead of `rest_info()` multiple times to get information for all collision (but not contact points or normals). Later I think the best would be to use `collide_shape()` and modify the physics server API to provide more information than just contact positions.

body: `_THREAD_SAFE_LOCK_` isn't a MutexLock, it's a `.lock()` call, so we need to be sure to `unlock()` it when the draw list is complete.
author: brianwinterpixel

body: I think there is a mix up here, 99% of the code base uses `_THREAD_SAFE_METHOD_` which makes sense to use here as well. `_THREAD_SAFE_METHOD_` automatically unlocks after the method is called (it uses a temporary variable that when it goes out of scope unlocks). It's a safer approach then using `_THREAD_SAFE_LOCK_` as you guarantee the lock being freed, while `_THREAD_SAFE_LOCK_` introduces the risk of exiting the method early and not unlocking.
author: BastiaanOlij

body:
Ah hang on, sorry guys, I misread this. It's two methods, `_draw_list_allocate`, in which we lock, and `_draw_list_free` in which we unlock. Then it does make sense to use `_THREAD_SAFE_LOCK_` and `_THREAD_SAFE_UNLOCK_` though. 

That said, it feels dangerous to me. There is a lot of potential here for a mismatch between lock and unlock. That one I'll leave to @reduz to comment on.

With these changes, it should work.

But I do not get why it's necessary at all. If it's `get_pos_at_line_column` should return only visible grapheme bounds, it's probably better to just get bounds and check if it's in the range, instead.

If the first and last character is visible, it doesn't necessarily mean all character in between are. Characters can be in the disconnected runs with different directions, e.g: `1|23987|654`,  where `|` is a screen bounds, last char is `9`, first is `2`, but `6`, `5` and `4` are not displayed.

body:
There are a lot more sensor types than just these four: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/hardware/Sensor#summary

As identified in #41421 we're currently calling Android's `((WindowManager)getActivity().getSystemService(WINDOW_SERVICE)).getDefaultDisplay()` and `display.getRotation()` every time there's a sensor event even when the display's rotation is not needed:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/1cbf3947d60e1edd39101ebd806d641d54cf53f1/platform/android/java/lib/src/org/godotengine/godot/Godot.java#L731-L734
And too many of these calls are causing a delay that can cause Input dispatching to timeout.

This PR addresses that problem by only calling it on the four sensor types that we're interested in and that need to be adjusted for the display's rotation.

body: `Ref<T>::operator=` does assign a pointer though, the one it wraps. And what we had in `PtrToArg::encode` in GodotCpp was really a pointer to `Ref<T>`, not the wrapped pointer... hence the pointer to pointer situation
author: Zylann

body:
It needs to do a lot more then assigning a pointer. It needs to check the current pointer that is being referenced and make sure that object is de-referenced, then assign the new pointer, then reference the object pointed to by the new pointer.

So 3 steps, and we were only doing 1 of the 3. 

The problem is that there is no operator= that takes an object pointer because within the context of Godot, this is illegal. The only scenario where you are using the pointer of a RefCounted object is on its construction. From that moment on you're only supposed to use `Ref<T>` to ensure we consistently update the refcounter.

Because we can't do this when exchanging objects between godot and godot-cpp because `Ref<T>` isn't portable between the two this fails.

Interestingly, Variant breaks this rule too so I need to have a closer look on how that works around it.
author: BastiaanOlij

Well I can imagine this function gets harder to write than the place we needed it since we are "further away" from the original use case in which the types of operands were pretty much known, now we have to do double-check everything which might be slower as well...

author: Zylann

body:
It's not just important to update the pointer, it's the refcount that is more important, especially from the object that may currently be there, which may be an object only known within `godot` and unknown to `godot-cpp`. 

The real problem here is that we have no info about what is currently held within and what is held within can't be released by `godot-cpp`. The new pointer we know everything about.

The big question is, is there ever a scenario where this code is used where the Ref isn't a brand new one and its existing pointer will thus be a nullptr and we're doing all this extra work for nothing.

body:
I think we need to figure out why this was commented out with a `?`, and whether attractors in 4.0 are supposed to have a `MASS` factor.

In `3.x` it's used this way:
```
$ rg -g'*.glsl' mass
drivers/gles3/shaders/particles.glsl
81:     float mass = 1.0;
192:                                    force += attractors[i].strength * rel_vec * attenuation * mass;
194:                                    force += attractors[i].strength * attractors[i].dir * attenuation * mass;
```
And there's indeed vertex shader code injected in-between so one can set `MASS` to something different from one to influence it.

In `master` there's also code for attractors, but they don't use use `mass` for now. Either they should be changed to use it, or the built-in should be removed. To me it looks like the current code purposely did not include `mass` anymore.

body:
It's a tricky one... it's a fix/workaround for the really far from perfect collision implementation.

Collision is something that I found more than whacky at the moment, strongly dependent on the particle system fps.
With the default 30 fps and some gravity, particles never come to a state where they stay in the "Collided" state and so the Turbulence continues to be applied. That looks really wrong and so this workaround was introduced.

When the collision implementation is getting a bit more love I'm pretty sure we can remove this.

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9423774/178154251-f5056aa4-c6e6-4042-ace9-e0c332cf1983.mp4
(Example of particles never coming to rest - no turbulence applied, just defaults. Red = !Collided, Green = Collided)

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9423774/178154294-3b901f42-3329-46c9-bddd-8e58f19b692b.mp4
(Example of how it would look without the workaround)

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9423774/178154307-02138d72-cc58-43d7-9e99-ef2ba1591f18.mp4
(Example with the workaround)


Overall collision needs some more work before it can considered "ready to use". It's pretty obvious when you start playing around with it.
author: RPicster

body:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/61245 should improve this significantly. That said, it's impossible for particles with collision to behave *exactly* the same regardless of fixed FPS. (This is also why I think a fixed FPS of 60 would be a better default, even with my PR merged.)

As a workaround, you can increase Fixed FPS to 1000 (it's different from setting it to 0 – I've found particles to behave better with 1000 compared to 0).

body:
In 3.x it uses the GL_LINES OpenGL primitive, which is indeed disconnected it looks like:

> GL_LINES: Vertices 0 and 1 are considered a line. Vertices 2 and 3 are considered a line. And so on. If the user specifies a non-even number of vertices, then the extra vertex is ignored.

https://www.khronos.org/opengl/wiki/Primitive

`width` and `anti-aliased` parameters are unused in 3.x. I'll try and have a look in 4.x and see if it is similar.

My guess is this was designed for e.g. drawing grids, but I don't know how often it is used, I can see it being used in animation track editor and audio stream editor. Compare to `add_polyline` which is for continuous rather than disjointed lines.

BTW on 3.x at least, this won't be that much faster than individual lines, as they are now batched. But this may be quite a bit faster for grids etc on 4.x as there is no batching.

EDIT: Looking at 4.x, it looks like thick lines are not yet supported, it may support multiple colors, but no idea beyond that as I have no familiarity with the vulkan renderer.

> Is there a physics overhead?

There should be no overhead on the physics side as long as it doesn't actually create new pairs (which should be the case with the cull check).

What I'm wondering is if we're going to have an overhead in the BVH itself if, let's say, you add lots of static bodies all at once in the broadphase. Even if they don't move later, they might cause an initial pairing check with each other.

It seems to me that the closest to the previous behavior in term of performance and functionality would be to:
-Start with using tree masks (but still with just 2 trees, static and non-static)
-Remove the object type thing (it wasn't really used anyway since objects were either paired with everything or nothing)
-Just return true in the cull check

And then in a separate PR, we can add one more tree and fix the area vs. static scenario.

I would be less worried for performance in some corner case scenarios this way.

body: Without the namespace, `Quaternion` references the method [`Quaternion()`](https://github.com/raulsntos/godot/blob/61253ff4131353150718ee1b8bc8505e6af127bd/modules/mono/glue/GodotSharp/GodotSharp/Core/Basis.cs#L609), at least in VSCode.

author: aaronfranke

body:
- The method `get_quaternion()` was added to C++ in 8861cc40fa79acd131875a556a8cf528384858ee (2017), it was a rename from the `operator Quaternion()` that has existed since Godot was made open source.
- The method `Quaternion()` was added to C# in #11899 (2017).
- The method `get_rotation_quaternion()` was added to C++ in #19193 (2018).
- The method `GetRotationQuaternion()` was added to C# in #22095 (2018) but as **internal**, it was later made **public** in #42293 (2020).

Also note that `GetRotationQuaternion()` internally calls `Quaternion()`.

Personally, since GDScript doesn't have the `Quaternion()` method I'm in favor of removing it or making it private and only expose `GetRotationQuaternion()` like in GDScript.

---

**EDIT:**

In C++:
- The `get_quaternion()` method which is public but not exposed to GDScript.
- The `operator Quaternion()` calls `get_quaternion()`.
- The `get_rotation_quaternion()` calls `get_quaternion()` and is exposed to GDScript.

In C#:
- The `Quaternion()` method should probably be renamed `GetQuaternion()` and since it's not exposed to GDScript we could make it **private**/**internal** in C# but maybe we want to keep it **public**.
- There are no conversion operators, we could implement explicit ones but this probably applies to all C# types, not just Basis.
- The `GetRotationQuaternion()` calls `Quaternion()` and is exposed, like in GDScript.

> There are no conversion operators, we could implement explicit ones but this probably applies to all C# types, not just Basis.

I think the conversion from `Basis` to `Quaternion` in GDScript is implicit. I'd prefer we don't add it to C#. I think implicit conversions are bad and should be used only where it improves code (like `NodePath`/`StringName` conversions from string); and the explicit operator adds little value when we already have the constructor.

body:
For `x86` and `arm` architectures, do we really need to change their nomenclature within the build configs?

Especially as `x86` usually indicates 32 bits, while `x86_64` indicates 64 bits. Similarly for `arm`, `armeabi-v7a` indicates 32 bits and `arm64-v8a` indicates 64 bits.

Seems like we can just use the same terms as used by everyone else instead of coming up with our own (`arm32`, `arm64`) terms.
author: m4gr3d

body: You'll also need to update the [`supportedAbis`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/15aea89868d16d0310a229d831e4a347a38dc1c3/platform/android/java/build.gradle#L24) values from which [`defaultAbi`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/15aea89868d16d0310a229d831e4a347a38dc1c3/platform/android/java/build.gradle#L32) is selected.
author: m4gr3d

body:
Yes, we should be explicit. 32-bit versions of these architectures are getting to be more and more niche and it's common to refer to both 32-bit and 64-bit versions of x86 as "x86". We want to avoid people wanting to build "for x86" or "for ARM" and accidentally building for what-will-be-ancient 32-bit versions of them. 

These terms are not dominant but they are not unique to Godot either, I've seen many usages of "x86_32" online. For ARM, there's a lot of names for them, the 64-bit version alone has "arm64v8", "aarch64", "armv8", "arm64-v8a", etc, it'd be better to use a simpler name that's easy to remember and harder to get confused with.

body:
I'm not sure what to do about the following (maybe something for documentation), but directly checking the reported memory heap doesn't always accurately portray available memory. 

For example, take these 3 reports:
1. [GTX 1650 SUPER](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displayreport.php?id=11718#memory): reports ~4GB of VRAM, ~8GB of other memory (RAM most likely), and ~200mb of some other device memory
2. [intel UHD 600](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displayreport.php?id=13359#memory): reports about 2GB of available memory (looks like RAM)
3. [intel HD 530](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displayreport.php?id=13337#memory): reports ~12GB of available memory (looks like RAM again)

Clearly "available memory" has 2 meanings, it can mean VRAM or it can mean RAM. This is a challenge for application designers, because your intel HD graphics driver may report having way more memory than your dedicated GPU. And just looking at the first memory heap that will indeed be the case. 

I am not sure whether this is a documentation issue for us or whether we need to have a more fine-grained approach to exposing memory (e.g. distinguishing between available memory - RAM + VRAM - and just VRAM)

author: derammo

body:
get_rule() operates off of GDScriptTokenizer's Token's Type enum, which does not match BinaryOpNode's Type list, and there is no mechanic to reverse engineer the token from which a Node came from.

So ultimately, using get_rule would:
- need to store the parser in a class variable
- need a function to translate the type of binary operator optype into a token type
- get the rule from the parser using the translation

So I feel it'd more complicated to set up the architecture there than it is just having a precedence rule function for this one node.

body: I agree.  I had searched poorly.  The code was referring to the token 'current' that is only transient during parsing, and the node never stores the precedence that it dereferences there.   That's too bad.   It still feels to me the facility you created is weird to exist outside the language definition.  If it is in fact possible to infer precedence JUST From a node type, then it should be possible to just have a table that maps from node types to token types and then look up the token in the parser.  That way, if the language changes you would get updates.   If you mapped multiple tokens, you could even check if there is any contradiction in your code.  Like if the language actually does NOT strictly sort those BinaryOpNode types because of context.  Just some ideas you might or might not find interesting.

Some comments:

- When the crash happens within the editor or project manager, the dump is saved in a project-specific folder. It should go to the editor data folder instead (`EditorPaths::get_data_dir()`).

- Could the dump filename be prefixed with an ISO 8601 timestamp? This would allow it to be sorted by date even if filesystem timestamps get overwritten for some reason (or when sharing the file to others).
  - For reference, we use `YYYY-MM-DDTHHMMSS` for editor screenshots (where `T` is a literal "T"). I suggest using the same format for consistency.

- I suggest rewording the message to make it easier to understand for people not familiar with Breakpad:
```
Breakpad crash dump created at: /path/to/crash.dmp
Please attach this file when reporting issues to the project developer.
```
  - Interestingly, GitHub doesn't allow uploading `.dmp` files in issue comments, even though the error message says it's one of the allowed extensions:
  > **We don’t support that file type.**
  > Try again with GIF, JPEG, JPG, MOV, MP4, PNG, SVG, WEBM, CPUPROFILE, CSV, DMP, DOCX, FODG, FODP, FODS, FODT, GZ, JSON, JSONC, LOG, MD, ODF, ODG, ODP, ODS, ODT, PATCH, PDF, PPTX, TGZ, TXT, XLS, XLSX or ZIP.

- `use_breakpad` is `False` by default, which means this feature is disabled by default. This might surprise people compiling from source, so maybe it should be enabled by default? I'm not sure, since official builds won't be able to benefit from it until [debugging symbols are distributed](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/1342) or at least preserved somewhere.

- Is the `use_breakpad` SCons option needed when there's `module_breakpad_enabled`, which could default to `False`? We do something similar for C#, where `module_mono_enabled` is `False` by default.

Note: It would probably be better to use a `poll()` to detect changes. However:
1. This is how the other thread is being managed; so I used this approach for consistency.
2. `poll()` should be used on both threads, but this would the require refactoring the `Joypad` class (separating the OS file descriptors from the Godot data to avoid `mutex` sharing) and is probably best done in a separate PR as an enhancement instead of a bug fix.
3. The other thread (as well as the [`XEvent` polling](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/d321858732c83f1aecfbc7e3de4c347cd509639e/platform/linuxbsd/display_server_x11.cpp#L3017)) uses a `select()` call (which is currently not used to detect changes, but [only to check whether a change has happened to prevent the next call from blocking](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/0462f7cacce57b35e7f4957ba95eb5514a3ad314/platform/x11/joypad_linux.cpp#L178-L184)). These `select()` calls should be replaced with `poll()` calls too. Again, this is best done in a separate PR as an enhancement.

body:
That would make sense if there was a single joypad and the purpose of the delay was to wait until there was new data. In reality the delay would be less than 8000 μs, because there is the time needed to read the data. The required delay would also be indeterminate if there were multiple joypads, because they wouldn't be synchronised.

Note: The purpose of this delay is to not be busy waiting; especially when there are no joypads attached.

body:
I can push the necessary changes to your branch later. Do you have a sample project I can use to validate the changes?

For reference on Android platforms, the Godot Engine runtime is spread between the main and render thread. The render thread is where the core of the engine runs, while the main thread is used for initial setup (`Godot.java`), input handling, and any other components/logic that interface with the underlying Android platform APIs.

In this PR, the `tts` calls are originating from the engine, and thus are running on the render thread. 
They cross the jni boundary and interact with the Android `TextToSpeech` api, so one of the first thing to check is to make sure that api can be called from the render thread.

In return the `TextToSpeech` api provides callbacks to notify of the state of the `tts` request, and these callbacks are routed back to the engine. So here we need to check which thread the `TextToSpeech` api uses to dispatch these callbacks and ensure they're routed back to the engine on the proper (render) thread.

Let me know if you have any questions.

body:
My main reason for not doing this is that the implementation is purely based on OpenXR, there really isn't a way to abstract things to some sort of template class that makes a lot of sense and especially for the vulkan extension, we'd be implementing far more on the dummy class while it is never even instantiated (the whole point is that if OpenXR is not available or not running, there will never be an instance).

This really is uniquely OpenXR and frankly frankenstein enough, while I understand why OpenXR went down this path, I really don't think they've architectures this very nicely. From a principled view they way OpenXR sets its hooks into Vulkan only makes sense for a purpose build XR engine.

body:
```suggestion
				Returns the 2D analog of the cross product for this vector and [code]with[/code].
				This is the signed area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors. If the second vector is clockwise from the first vector, then the cross product is the positive area. If counter-clockwise, the cross product is the negative area.
```

I'm not sure that the `[b]Note:[/b]` part is helpful. Do Godot users care about how something is originally defined by mathematicians for usage in 3D, or do they care about how it's defined in 2D and in Godot? We are already saying that Vector2's cross method is the closest analog to the cross product.

The cross product in 2D is an extension of the original 3D definition, losing the property of the resulting vector being perpendicular to both input vectors (which is impossible in 2D unless the two vectors are colinear but then the cross product is zero anyway) (plus the result isn't a vector). It's the closest analog that exists.

We could keep both explanations if it's helpful for people to understand.

We could also note for Vector3 that the magnitude of the cross product vector is the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors. For 3D, we don't have to worry about signed area because that's just indicated by which direction the output vector points.

body: An important distinguishing feature of simplex noise over other gradient noise types is that the gradients exist in a simplex lattice rather than a grid lattice. This helps avoid directional artifacts that perlin noise suffers from. It also means that it scales better with an increase in dimensions (once you hit 4 or more dimensions simplex noise becomes much faster than perlin)

body:
We had a lengthy discussion about this in today's PR review meeting. The consensus was to merge this for now and then evaluate user feedback during the alphas and betas. With the new noise abstract class, it seems like FastNoise would be a great fit for a first-class GDExtension, but the GDExtension system is still relatively new, and we want to get this in the engine and get user feedback now.

Depending on user feedback, (i.e. if users find the current options too complicated) we are considering exposing a simpler type of noise only by default and then exposing the full range of noise types and parameters in an official GDExtension. 

To merge this, the documentation needs to be finished.

One other consideration is ``get_noise_4d()`` I don't like taking away a function that was available in 3.x. Is there any way that we can implement something on top of FastNoise that exposes ``get_noise_4d()``?

body:
So how it worked was that you get two lists, just own properties and all the properties including parent classes. Both are reported in their bind order, similar to inspector. Then we iterate the list of all properties. The assumption is that the list of all properties contains all the own properties first. So by the time `EO` is null, the own properties have ended and it is safe to assume every other property is inherited.

While `EO` is true we compare the values (below) and move the cursor one position forward. This still works when I add sorting, but the caveat is that we can no longer assume that own properties are the first ones. They still follow the same order, just have gaps of inherited properties in between. So we can no longer use that old default value, but it's safe to default to `true` instead. Every own property will be caught by the check below, as long as there is anything left to check.

body:
I was having unexplained corruption with some texture dimensions and traced it to these returned width/height values (returned by `Image::get_image_mipmap_offset_and_dimensions`).

For example, on the 12x12 texture (block=4), I was seeing this. First loop iteration
```
{
  bw=12, bh=12
  s=144
  w = 6, h = 6
  *r_mm_width = (12>>1) = 6
  *r_mm_height = (12>>1) = 6
}
```
Second loop iteration
```
{
  bw=8, bh=8
  s=64
  w = 3, h = 3
  *r_mm_width = (8>>1) = 4 <-- wrong!
  *r_mm_height = (8>>1) = 4 <-- wrong!
}
```
Third loop iteration
```
{
  bw=4, bh=4
  s=16
  w = 1, h = 1
  *r_mm_width = (4>>1) = 2 <-- wrong!
  *r_mm_height = (4>>1) = 2 <-- wrong!
}
```

Note that the behavior of this function was altered slightly by 81ed9fa31bc63823235f64c88d441a8e530ab039
However, It was also wrong before. It's possible either that Godot always had this bug with 2x2 and 1x1 mipmaps reading out-of-bounds, or didn't cause an issue before because the old `etc` compression library ignored the out-of-bounds data.

I can't see any reason for the return values to use these "half-block" values. I would think if I want to know the dimensions of a mipmap level, I would want the actual dimensions, namely `w` and `h`. I can't find any callers of this code which would be adversely affected by this change.

In case you want to check my assertions, the only public functions using these `*r_mm_` return values are `Image::get_image_mipmap_size` and `Image::get_image_mipmap_offset_and_dimensions`.

I did some further digging into that logic, so a quick history breakdown. @reduz originally added this `*r_mm_width = bw;` statement in 0586e184490fd132f99acb1a67c788959cfdbade . This function was only used in one place, in what is now `servers/rendering/renderer_rd/renderer_storage_rd.cpp`. However, the function was only ever used with FORMAT_RGBA8 for the longest time, meaning block size is 1 and bw == w and bh == h. For this reason, I suspect reduz either never tested it with compressed formats, or had a different intended usecase in mind than what it has ultimately been used for.

Alright, I know I talk too much. I hope this answers your question about why this code change was necessary, why it was relevant to this PR, and why it evaded notice for so long. I'll also loop in @floppyhammer as they made the more recent commit here.

This description is true but it might be not descriptive enough as:

>relative to the origin of the [CanvasLayer] that this [CanvasItem] is in

doesn't state in what way it's relative to the origin (origin is just a point). It may be not obvious that the returned position is described in the given `CanvasLayer`'s basis vectors. Meaning if that `CanvasLayer` is anyhow rotated, scaled, skewed, etc. (in other words when its basis is not standard) then there still might be some confusion about the result.

A description like:

>Returns the mouse's position in the coordinate space of the [CanvasLayer] that this [CanvasItem] is in.

doesn't have this issue (at least I think so) but it's probably not user-friendly as there are many no-math users (_"what is coordinate space?!"_). Maybe such description would be good if "coordinate space" would link to some page describing what it means? :thinking: 

My point is that current descriptions (the same issue with the other similar changes) are not fully descriptive. There's still missing information (relative in what way?) in them. I can't find wording to be both descriptive ("in the coordinate space") and user-friendly ("relative to") in a compact way. Maybe you could come up with something like that.

body:
Technically, we should be using the same formula as with shadow sizes above the default. However, this would result in too much peter-panning, so I went for a half-way compromise between not adjusting the bias at all and adjusting it to match the resolution perfectly.

The bias factors used for each resolution are:

- 256: `8.5`
- 512: `4.5`
- 1024: `2.5`
- 2048: `1.5`
- 4096: `1.0`
- 8192: `0.5`
- 16384: `0.25`

This applies to both directional and point light shadows.
author: Calinou

body:
This logic should be different for Point Light Shadows, as you have to have the resolution of the cell the shadow is using, not the entire shadow map.

This would incorrectly change bias for the same effective resolution of shadow if you go from a 4k shadow map with 4 4 4 4 quadrants and change to 8k shadow map resolution with 16 16 16 16 quadrants which effectively results in same resolution, just more shadows available.

I know this is already merged but I decided to look over it anyway and I give it a ✅

Everything in this PR falls into one of these 3 categories:

* The float literal has an identical value to the double literal (such as sums of powers of two `0.5f` or integers `0.0f`, `1.0f`, etc)

* The value is in Color, which should be always 32-bit anyway (since more precision is useless for Color)

body:
There seems to be a inconsistency between the Gradle and SCons targets.

"Debug" template *are* built with `scons tools=no target=release_debug`. The `target=debug` platform is only used for actual engine debugging (i.e. getting dev asserts, more information on crashes, etc.), and we don't ship any binaries built with `target=debug` (this is only for custom builds for people who know they need it).

I see that `platform/android/detect.py` doesn't seem to do anything special for `target=release_debug` compared to `target=release`, which is a discrepancy with all other platforms (note that it's `startswith`, applies to both `release` and `release_debug`): https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f5b9cbaff6f0a058d08187b3124948ae68848cd0/platform/android/detect.py#L189
author: akien-mga

body:
That doesn't match the build matrix for other platforms.

The official released (production) editor binaries use `target=release_debug`. The editor can't be used with `target=release` only, as debugging tools are then not included, and it would crash on errors instead of reporting them.

So the only two editor targets you should support are:
`tools=yes target=release_debug` -> production build, official releases
`tools=yes target=debug` -> development build, used by engine developers (slow and not meant for use in production)

```suggestion
    if os.access("bin/godot" + suffix, os.F_OK) and not os.access("bin/godot" + suffix, os.W_OK):
```

```suggestion

						(-p_pre + 3.0f * p_from - 3.0f * p_to + p_post) * (p_weight * p_weight * p_weight));
```

body:
I don't think this is the right solution. It seems like any time that `bisection_page == before_page_inclusive` automatically becomes a failure case because the method is called again with `bisection_page + 1` as `after_page_inclusive` which means the base case of `before_page_inclusive == after_page_inclusive` is never triggered because in that scope, `before_page_inclusive` is greater than `after_page_inclusive`. Satisfying that constraint is impossible. Could we try making the base case `before_page_inclusive >= after_page_inclusive` instead of using `==`?

If we do that though, it's not immediately clear to me whether we should return `before_page_inclusive` or `after_page_inclusive` in the base case. It could cause problems if we return the wrong one, because it could possibly be an empty page. Although, an empty page isn't the end of the world because playback should handle those gracefully.

I'm really sorry for how confusing this code is. My head is spinning trying to understand it now, months later.

body:
In the MRP, it's kind of like searching for pos 0 inside index range `[0, 2]`:

| idx | pos | size |
|------|------|-------|
| 0     | 0     | 1     |
| 1     | 0     | 0     |
| 2     | 0     | 1     |

body:
It's likely that somewhere in the engine the value can get truncated to 32-bit floats. Having a stricter epsilon can be useful for debugging, but I wouldn't enable it by default.

```suggestion
#ifdef PRECISE_MATH_CHECKS
		return abs(s) < CMP_EPSILON_64;
#else
		return abs(s) < CMP_EPSILON;
#endif // PRECISE_MATH_CHECKS
```
author: aaronfranke

body:
The ideal epsilon for 64-bit floats is not the same as the epsilon for 32-bit floats squared. It's about `1e-14` or `0.00000000000001`.

Also, the current epsilon value for 32-bit floats could theoretically have an extra zero added since the ideal is about `1e-6`, but it's a risky change to do if something depends on the extra leniency. I'm not sure that I would bother defining `CMP_EPSILON_32` if it's just the same as `CMP_EPSILON`, but maybe this is a good opportunity to introduce a stricter epsilon value for 32-bit floats.

```suggestion
#define CMP_EPSILON_32 0.000001
#define CMP_EPSILON_64 0.00000000000001
```
author: aaronfranke

body: IMO, if the `double` version of `is_zero_approx` is used in a version of Godot compiled with doubles, and yet you want such a high epsilon to be used *by default* due to some kind of truncation, it means the code calling it is wrong, or it should be using the `float` version all the time, or should use a custom threshold. These unusual cases should be explicit. I don't think hiding the issue solves it.
author: Zylann

body:
All good points, but I am thinking it would be a risky change. As you mentioned, some code calling it could be wrong, or somewhere down the line some piece of code can be truncating to 32-bit floats. It seems like these kinds of problems are worth finding and fixing, but doing it by default seems risky if a bug appears in production. Also, this `double` method is available to builds of Godot where real_t is float.

I think we'll have to ask @akien-mga or @reduz what their thoughts are on this.
author: aaronfranke

body:
Zylann has convinced me that we do need to use the stricter double tolerance in the `is_equal_approx` and `is_zero_approx` methods that uses doubles.

If we decide to keep the methods as they are in this PR, with the double methods using an epsilon more precise than what 32-bit floats are expected to have in error, it would still be a nice idea to have stricter epsilon values available when bug hunting.

```suggestion
#ifdef PRECISE_MATH_CHECKS
#define CMP_EPSILON_32 0.000001
#define CMP_EPSILON_64 0.00000000000001
#else
#define CMP_EPSILON_32 0.00001
#define CMP_EPSILON_64 0.000000001
#endif // PRECISE_MATH_CHECKS
```
author: aaronfranke

body: True, it depends how we want to see `CMP_EPSILON`, because it really isn't THE epsilon from `float` and `double` numbers, it's rather some sort of convenience one that got implicitely used everywhere since every decimal number was a float, but because of that it's getting problematic to decide how to fix problems when we actually have large doubles to deal with.

body:
Yes. To keep it simple, the Time singleton does not deal with timezone offsets or suffixes, so including them manually is the way to do it (assuming you do in fact need the offset).

However, note that it's convention to not put a space between the timestamp and offset (so it would be `"%s%s"`), and for zero offset it's common to abbreviate this to `Z` (so if `p_offset_minutes` is zero, we can optionally do a version with `"%sZ"`)

Another consideration, we could potentially shorten this using `get_time_string_from_unix_time`, or maybe there should be a dedicated method for converting an offset number to a string - even if the rest of the methods are unaware of timezones, we can add a method to do the same logic you're doing here for the suffix. We just need to think about things like if we want it to print `Z` or `+00:00` and if we want the input value to be in minutes or seconds.
author: aaronfranke

author: aaronfranke

body:
Thanks for adding the offset to string conversion to `Time`, I will rebase this PR once that change is merged. 

The reason for me not going for a `%sZ%s` is that Git usually shows the `<space>+05:30` format rather than the one with a `Z`, so I will probably just change it to directly use the offset to string conversion function. 

Since the VCS integration is closely (but not directly) mimicing Git, for the time being I am trying to incorporate "Git-likeness" in it if it seems fine, and that is up until the time where we work on other VCS plugins that would require us to further generalise the time format used in the VCS integration in the future, amongst tons of other generalizations that we'd need to make in the UI.

body:
For numeric types, from what I read it seems that using `type="text" inputmode="..."` is a better option. Using `type="number"` sanitizes `elem.value` to a floating point number (or empty) per the [HTML spec](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#number-state-(type=number)). We should leave number parsing/validation to Godot users if they want it.

For `type="url"` and `type="email"`, the browser is also supposed to sanitize `value` by stripping leading and trailing whitespace. This isn't as invasive as `type="number"` so I think it's okay to use?

I'll switch to using `type` for the rest.

This project setting doesn't seem to be read when it's changed at run-time, so the effective global panning strength can't be changed at run-time (changes will be ignored). body:
I'm not fond of adding exceptions (as they might be forgotten when other things change), but in this case the proper solution would be quite complex, so doing this is be fine. Just the suggested change should be enough.

For reference, the actual problem is that the `int()` constructor has multiple signatures with the same number of parameters but different types. GDScript find the `int(int from)` constructor first, so it thinks the parameter has a narrowing conversion. GDScript should prefer the `int(float from)` constructor, but to do so it would require to know about the multiple types and choose the best match based on those.

It's not something trivial to add, and not really necessary, so for now it's okay to have the exception.

body:
Since there is no C# counterpart, the GDScript-specific codeblock should be removed. Also, singular `[codeblock]` tag should be used instead:

```suggestion
				[codeblock]
				# Like this string, the placeholders may be replaced in steps.
				var str = "The NPC, named {npc_name}, is {npc_age} years old, he comes from $1, and is a member of [organization_name]..."
				# You may already get the npc info like this.
				var npc_info = {"npc_name": "Tom", "npc_age": 24, "organization_id":021, "npc_equipments": {"head": 001, "left_hand": 012}}
				# As the placeholder is the default one, so we can just format `str` like this.
				str = str.format(npc_info) # "The NPC, named Tom, is 24 years old, he comes from $1, and is a member of [organization_name]..."

				# The list of places may look like this.
				var places = ["GodotDesert", "MountGodot", "GodotRiver", "GodotLake"]
				# This placeholder is "$_" now.
				str = str.format(places, "$_") # "The NPC, named Tom, is 24 years old, he comes from MountGodot, and is a member of [organization_name]..."

				# May find the organization info like this.
				var org_info = [["id", 1 ], ["organization_name", "A"], ["position", 1], ["members", []]]
				# The placeholder now is "[_]".
				str = str.format(org_info, "[_]") # "The NPC, named Tom, is 24 years old, he comes from MountGodot, and is a member of A..."
				[/codeblock]
```

Otherwise, no code block will appear at all if the user chose to display only C# code blocks. This can be confusing.

On second thought, the code sample actually seems hard to follow for me. I find the comments quite confusing as well, especially since the dictionaries/arrays contain unrelated information. Therefore, I think it would be better to showcase a *minimal* example, even if it's less comprenhensive. Something like:

```gdscript
var string = "The NPC {name} lives in {location}.".format({"name": "Tom", "location": "the village"})
print(string)  # The NPC Tom lives in the village.
```

I wouldn't bother showcasing custom placeholders within the class reference, as it's a very situational use case. 99% of the time, standard named placeholders are all you need, including for internationalization :slightly_smiling_face: 

Also, `str` is not a valid variable name (it's a reserved built-in function), so it should be renamed to `string`.

body:
It seems like a mistake to require both ABS L and R in order to determine whether a device is a gamepad or not. This definition will leave a lot of devices unsupported that people would expect (previously mentioned joycons, for example.)

My 2 cents on the matter here is that we should probably take a page out of SDLs book and be more pragmatic about classifying the feature-set of a given device before filtering the device. We then create a few different masks that we deem to be the "bare minimum gamepad" based on some of the gamepads on the market that have limited feature sets. Additionally, we should consider making a "excludes from gamepad" mask that filters out problematic devices that often have some input overlap with game controllers (drawing tablets, etc.)

So the breakdown of what should be done here on a design level

- Create an enum listing all possible device features that forms a mask. This includes buttons, axis, touch screen, touch pad, stylus, etc. 
- Create a method that returns the feature set of a given device with a breakdown of all possible features. It is worth noting in the function name that this is a guess, not a concrete definition and all future modification to guess work would need to be done in this given method. 
- Define a constant that defines a (few) minimum viable controllers. For example, we currently (in master) would have a set of the following minimum requirements  `HAS_KEYS | HAS_AXIS | HAS_AXIS_LEFT` and `HAS_KEYS | HAS_AXIS | HAS_AXIS_RIGHT`. This creates a easy to parse minimum set of required features for contributors to modify later as more edge cases crop up. 
- Define a constant that defines a feature blacklist. Any device that has these features are automatically removed from being considered valid. For example, filtering out tablets would involve filtering devices with `HAS_STYLUS`. This gives us a concrete list of features that we decide as a group as being "exclusive" from being considered a game controller. 
- Algorithm of `open_joypad` would roughly follow the logic of 
  - Guess feature-set by calling previously mentioned method; Base the logic of guesses off SDL procedure if necessary.
  - Match against any minimum viable controller flag combo, return and close if we don't match any of the minimum requirements.
  - Return and Close device if we match against any gamepad feature on the blacklist. This will help remove laptop touch screens and graphics tablets from listings.

So, in short, I think that we should design from the ground up with regards to improving the input situation and start by trying to get a better understanding of the USB device's entire feature-set before attempting to enforce rules.

body:
```suggestion
		[EditorUndoRedoManager] is a manager for [UndoRedo] objects associated with edited scenes. Each scene has its own undo history and [EditorUndoRedoManager] ensures that each action performed in the editor gets associated with a proper scene. For actions not related to scenes ([ProjectSettings] edits, external resources, etc.), a separate global history is used.
		The usage is mostly the same as [UndoRedo]. You create and commit actions and the manager automatically decides under-the-hood what scenes it belongs to. The scene is deduced based on the first operation in an action, using the object from the operation. The rules are as follows:
		- If the object is a [Node], use the currently edited scene;
		- If the object is a built-in resource, use the scene from its path;
		- If the object is external resource or anything else, use global history.
		This guessing can sometimes yield false results, so you can provide a custom context object when creating an action.
```

body:
So for Emscripten I found out that `-msse*` flags can be passed too.

Here's a test with:
```
#ifdef __SSE2__
#error yay sse
#endif

int main() { return 0; }
```
```
$ emcc main.c -msse4.2
emcc: error: passing any of -msse, -msse2, -msse3, -mssse3, -msse4.1, -msse4.2, -msse4, -mavx, -mavx2, -mfpu=neon flags also requires passing -msimd128 (or -mrelaxed-simd)!
~/tmp/godot/embree (master %)$ emcc main.c -msse4.2 -msimd128
main.c:2:2: error: yay sse
    2 | #error yay sse
      |  ^
1 error generated.
emcc: error: '/home/akien/Godot/toolchains/emsdk/upstream/bin/clang -target wasm32-unknown-emscripten -fignore-exceptions -mllvm -combiner-global-alias-analysis=false -mllvm -enable-emscripten-sjlj -mllvm -disable-lsr --sysroot=/home/akien/Godot/toolchains/emsdk/upstream/emscripten/cache/sysroot -DEMSCRIPTEN -D__SSE__=1 -D__SSE2__=1 -D__SSE3__=1 -D__SSSE3__=1 -D__SSE4_1__=1 -D__SSE4_2__=1 -Xclang -iwithsysroot/include/fakesdl -Xclang -iwithsysroot/include/compat -msimd128 -c main.c -o /tmp/emscripten_temp_jpbtn1l3/main_0.o' failed (returned 1)
```

As you can see on the error line it does set relevant `__SSE*__` flags when passing those args.

This matches what's described on https://emscripten.org/docs/porting/simd.html#compiling-simd-code-targeting-x86-sse-instruction-sets, that we should pass one of these flags together with `-msimd128`. So we could consider setting `-msse4.2` for wasm32 too.

Discussion in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106319#discussion_r2087141916 (it would need to be disabled for etcpak).

Again this would be for a follow-up PR, it's good if this one keeps its focus on x86_64 and doesn't impact other targets.

I don't think it's a good idea to add spaces to words that don't have any underscores in them. If I saw "Comment Focus" in the inspector, my inclination would be to type `comment_focus` into a script because in every other property, a space indicates an underscore. That could be confusing for users, so it would be better to rename these properties to include an underscore where needed instead of "fake" renaming them here.

This goes for "commentfocus", "defaultfocus", "defaultframe", "hseparation", "selectedframe", "vadjust", and "separation" (and "normalmap" as well, but that one wasn't done by this PR)

I'm not sure. We decided to remap things like `vsync` to `V-Sync` and `po2` to `Power of 2` at the very beginning.

The real property path is visible in tooltip and copyable via context menu or dragging to script directly. IMHO, the capitalization process is more like doing extra English localization from the property-name language. It's not guaranteed to be able to convert back.

And it's not always able to convert back even without the remapping process: e.g. both `http_2` and `http2` are `Http 2` after naive capitalization.

I tested it and it works really well. Just a few things need to be changed/fixed:
* The editor grid drawing should be changed to respect `cell_shape` and `cell_offset_axis` settings like the TileMap editor grid does.
* `cell_offset_axis` only works in hexagon mode, so you can't use offset squares like you can in TileMaps.

TreeItem should have a second property called `parent_visible_in_tree` which is set when TreeItem is added to Tree. The first TreeItem has it always as true, then its children will have `parent_visible_in_tree` true if the parent has both `visible` and `parent_visible_in_tree` set to true. This is great work :trophy: .
With the merge of #66938 we should start moving debugger functionalities out of core and into modules.
I think this is a great candidate for that.
We should move the new files (`editor/debugger/editor_expression_evaluator.cpp`, and `editor/debugger/editor_expression_evaluator.cpp`) into a dedicated module (which I suggest we name "debugger_console" since we might want to add more feature to it).

This will keep things clean, and allow to easily disable the plugin in release builds.

There is an example in `modules/multiplayer/editor/multiplayer_editor_plugin.cpp`, but **I can help with the porting if you want**, just let me know.
One tricky thing is the category name which is hardcoded. We can leave it as "Unknown" initially, but we should probably pass the string directly instead of an int which has to be later interpreted.

One extra note, the PR re-adds 2 files which should be completely removed: `modules/visual_script/visual_script.cpp` and `modules/visual_script/visual_script.h`.

body:
> Using 33 was a typo here AFAICT, it should be 63 like the multiplier, which is what fits in 6 bits.

Yeah, definitely a typo.

> However comparing the RGB565 conversion with RGBA4444, and some sources online, I have the feel that one of the two is handling the channels backwards. Needs to sit down and write the math, or do some tests, I suspect more fixes are needed.

AFAICT it's correct for RGBA4444, and here it's doing BGR565 instead of RGB565 (BTW the variable should be renamed `rgba` -> `rgb`).

E.g. here you can compare R5G6B5 vs B5G6R5:
- https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/1.3-extensions/man/html/VkFormat.html#_description
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/dxgiformat/ne-dxgiformat-dxgi_format#constants

`Image::_get_color_at_ofs` decodes these in the same order as they're set in here though.
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fe01776f05b1787b28b4a270d53037a3c25f4ca2/core/io/image.cpp#L3116-L3130

So if using `set_pixel`/`get_pixel` etc. it should work fine, but if creating an image from a byte buffer / obtaining such buffer from the image then the results could be unexpected for FORMAT_RGB565 as internally the buffer is assumed to be B5G6R5, not R5G6B5.

Not sure if chaning this is feasible at this point, or if it should be just documented in detail.

body:
Two problems here:
1. Using a lower form of PCF for further splits results on visibly worse quality shadows, I don't think we should force that on users
2. Sampling textures in if/else blocks can be a problem on older GPUs as the GPU ends up running both sides of the branch (and thus waiting on the results of both texture lookups). There is a reason this section of code is structured to do the texture lookups after the branching. On high-end GPUs the difference likely won't be noticable, but on low end or older GPUs this can really hurt performance. 

A better approach is to do what you did in 4.0 and adjust the ``directional_shadow_pixel_size`` based on which split you are in. This avoids both issues above and should result in the same benefits as your 4.0 PR.

Maybe it's better to add a return argument to the macro:

```c++
#define VALIDATE_YMDHMS(ret)                                                                                                                                              \
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(month == 0, ret, "Invalid month value of: " + itos(month) + ", months are 1-indexed and cannot be 0. See the Time.Month enum for valid values."); \
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(month > 12, ret, "Invalid month value of: " + itos(month) + ". See the Time.Month enum for valid values.");                                       \
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(hour > 23, ret, "Invalid hour value of: " + itos(hour) + ".");                                                                                    \
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(minute > 59, ret, "Invalid minute value of: " + itos(minute) + ".");                                                                              \
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(second > 59, ret, "Invalid second value of: " + itos(second) + " (leap seconds are not supported).");                                             \
	/* Do this check after month is tested as valid. */                                                                                                                   \
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(day == 0, ret, "Invalid day value of: " + itos(month) + ", days are 1-indexed and cannot be 0.");                                                 \
	uint8_t days_in_this_month = MONTH_DAYS_TABLE[IS_LEAP_YEAR(year)][month - 1];                                                                                         \
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(day > days_in_this_month, ret, "Invalid day value of: " + itos(day) + " which is larger than the maximum for this month, " + itos(days_in_this_month) + ".");
```

body:
Well for `SceneShaderGLES2::FADE_TO` I couldn't help noticing we have already sent this value 5 lines above (as `split_offsets`), and each uniform is additional extra API (especially in GLES2), and can compete for limited space in GPU for highly cached stuff.

The only question is which of these 4 is the furthest split, but I'm presuming this must have been previously calculated in the shader (for it to have worked previously).

There are 2 questions that appear:
* Is it more expensive to use the existing `if` clauses than to send as an independent additional uniform (this may be the case, dynamic branches aren't good but maybe we have paid the price already)
* The existing `light_split_offset` is stored as `highp`. This might not be necessary for the calculation so could maybe be downcast.

I guess these can only be answered by performance testing especially on mobile. And I guess could be left to a follow up. I'm not sure whether this was considered in 4.x, but maybe there were additional factors at play.

body:
Rather than checking for specific languages' extensions, it's better to use `ResourceLoader::get_resource_type(p_path)` to extract a typename and then use an inheritance check to see if it inherits from the `Script` class. If so, you know it's a script, regardless of what language it is.

You can *probably* assume that a user-defined type WON'T be an implementation of a Script, so you could skip it, but ordinarily, you would first check `ScriptServer::is_global_class()` and then based on that either use `EditorNode::get_editor_data().script_class_is_parent()` if true or `ClassDB::is_parent_class()` if false. Note also that you can only use the former if you are in an editor context. If it's something that would be running in a live application outside the editor, then you have to fully load the script and then do `script->get_language()->get_global_class_name(script->get_path())`. It's a bit ridiculous, just because the ScriptServer doesn't do any work to maintain a reverse lookup of path-to-typename.
author: willnationsdev

Nor if I chose to define a second type extending my first one. body: @Atlinx Also, I just realized examining this, that this is not really a good solution (or at least, it doesn't seem very reliable). Any given file can have 0 or more dependencies, any number of which might happen to be a script. But you don't know *which* of those dependencies is the `script` property of the file in question. So, imo, you really *do* need to have some sort of resource script type property being tracked in the `FileInfo`/`FileCache` in `EditroFileSystem`. And rather than forcing the use of `ResourceFormatLoaderText`, you would need to define a virtual function in `ResourceFormatLoader` that gets the scripted type of the resource, if it has one, which you would then override in the various derived implementations. Then the logic to get the file's resource script type would involve iterating over all of the loaders present in the `ResourceLoader`.
