Did you perhaps mean that the script will always be *last*? Because I have a use case in my sample project for #48201 where an exported resource property itself uses a global script class that has another global script class property as its exported property, and in *that* use case, there are 2 `[ext_resource type="Script"...]` tags with the bottom one being the `script` property's `Script` (i.e. the "attached" script). Which then results in @Atlinx's code triggering a bug in my code.

To be specific, my demo has a `Tile2D` node that has a `terrain` property of type `Terrain`. It is possible to load a `WildTerrain` resource onto it (or an `UrbanTerrain`), and the `WildTerrain` has an exported array of `NaturalResource` resources. And in this use case, if I save e.g. a `wild_terrain_1.tres` file, that file needs both `NaturalResource` and `WildTerrain`, but it grabs the wrong one b/c `WildTerrain` is at the bottom and it stops after it finds the first one.

The result is that the `QuickLoad` popup is unable to find the saved resource file because it does not perceive the file to have the `WildTerrain` type.

Either way, this PR needs to be amended to fix that.

body:
(Edit: lol, I started writing this before I saw that you had already responded and seem perfectly at ease with the feedback, but anyway, just in case, I hope you find this explanation helpful, haha)

I wanna thank you again for all the work you put into this PR. Even if it isn't accepted in its current state, it definitely gives a better starting point from which to create a more effective solution.

I've been in past situations where I did a bunch of work for a PR and received a similar response of my changes being too "invasive" or "hacky". At the time, I was quite disheartened and frustrated. This may or may not be the case for you, but if it is, I'm re-reviewing these changes through this lens to consider in what ways others may find fault with them. I hope my feedback can provide insight into what could be improved here and enrich the quality of your future work should you choose to continue making contributions.

- For things labeled as "comment bloat":

    Generally, Godot's source code only contains comments when it is meant to explain *why* the chosen code was selected vs. another approach since it usually is a contextual matter specific to Godot's codebase/behavior. That is, one needs to take into account other code in order to know why the current code is doing what it does.
    
    However, if the current code is self-explanatory or can be discerned simply by reading the code within the class/function and putting the pieces together yourself, then explanatory comments are avoided since they are a maintenance hazard; they can easily become outdated by future contributors' work, and they unnecessarily space out the code making it harder to read as much content within a single view.

- For things labeled as "uncertain/questionable core bloat*" or "core bloat?*":

    This is a pull request that relates to improving the behavior of things at the editor level. As such, the effect it should have on the engine's core should be kept to a minimum. However, in the case of this specific problem, it ultimately has to be resolved by extracting serialized data from resources which, in turn, must involve making changes to the way in which resources are serialized (a piece of core logic). So you can't really *avoid* making *some* core changes to implement a solution (I **think**). If there IS a way to do that, then we need to investigate that possibility and re-work the solution to support that. If not though, I don't personally see any issue with the way you've added the extra behavior to the `ResourceFormatLoader`(s). Rather, the more pertinent issue is probably...(next point)
    
- For things labeled as "core bloat**":

    Variant is an extremely core class since it basically touches every piece of the engine, so any changes made to it are done so with great care. Nonetheless, there are a variety of new methods you've added to its parser which I'm not entirely sure should be necessary just for the sake of implementing this feature.

    Furthermore, the way in which the type information is extracted using the tags is inherently "hacky" since it revolves around figuring out where the list of property tags are, iterating through all of the properties, and identifying which one corresponds to the object's "script" property. This in turn makes the logic entirely dependent on the structural makeup of the tag tree, as well as whether the object in question has a "script" property. Should a later alteration in the engine choose to modify how script information is associated with an object, the VariantParser, of all things, would now suddenly be broken (which would not be directly related to Object-handling code and thus not obvious).
    
    In addition, the algorithm introduces a linear-time operation over the number of properties the object serializes. This contrasts with how, in concept at least, the operation is not at all requesting aggregate data related to the object's properties. It would make more sense for it to be constant-time operation.

None of this is to suggest that you didn't have reasons for doing things the way you did. I honestly probably would've first thought to do something similar to what you did (which is probably why I didn't question it the first time I reviewed it). That is, don't make any major changes to the way data is tracked and just work with what is already there to accomplish what minimum changes are necessary to make the logic further down the pipeline work properly.

In theory, you are attempting to avoid making significant changes to the core. In practice though, given the lengths your implementation has to go through to get things to work as needed, a worrying number of changes are introduced.

In this PR, you introduce changes to the core variant logic *merely* to support this one higher-level feature. If left alone and accepted, such single-purpose solutions culminate in a codebase that has many small pieces in the core that are not actually used by or relevant to the core at all, thus leading to code bloat. It would be preferred if we could make the minimum number of changes possible to the core to expose whatever information is necessary for higher-level pieces of the codebase to implement the required logic. This shifts the bulk of the changes to later layers of the architecture and results in a simpler and more direct approach to achieving the same goal.

I appreciate you going through all the effort of writing and maintaining this branch. It will certainly be a big help in guiding the direction of the next attempt at fixing this issue. Great work!

Note that these angles are in radians so they can't really be exactly 180 degrees apart (180 degrees = PI radians and PI is irrational). Meaning in such cases the actual difference is always a little smaller/bigger than 180 degrees (by some epsilon).

No idea what do you mean by "_through the negative side_", it's not clear. I'd say it can lerp either clockwise or counter-clockwise. > And I think whether it goes clockwise/counter-clockwise depends of the error I've mentioned earlier (whether the actual angle difference is bigger/smaller than 180 degrees).

In practice it's when this is called with a difference of `PI` that the UB happens. But indeed due to floating point precision the result can basically be one or the other, depending on whether `fmod(nearly TAU, TAU)` ends up as "nearly `TAU`" or "nearly 0". So it's not so much an implementation details as unpredictable.

body:
>when these two angles are approximately [constant @GDScript.PI] apart

To be precise: if angles are `PI + k * TAU` apart for any integer `k`. For example `0` and `99 * PI` angles are also kinda `PI` apart.

```
i=0  COUNTER-CLOCKWISE    lerp_angle(0, PI + 0 * TAU, 0.5) = -1.570796
i=1  COUNTER-CLOCKWISE    lerp_angle(0, PI + 1 * TAU, 0.5) = -1.570796
i=2  COUNTER-CLOCKWISE    lerp_angle(0, PI + 2 * TAU, 0.5) = -1.570796
i=3  COUNTER-CLOCKWISE    lerp_angle(0, PI + 3 * TAU, 0.5) = -1.570796
i=4  COUNTER-CLOCKWISE    lerp_angle(0, PI + 4 * TAU, 0.5) = -1.570796
i=5  CLOCKWISE            lerp_angle(0, PI + 5 * TAU, 0.5) =  1.570796
i=6  COUNTER-CLOCKWISE    lerp_angle(0, PI + 6 * TAU, 0.5) = -1.570796
i=7  CLOCKWISE            lerp_angle(0, PI + 7 * TAU, 0.5) =  1.570796
i=8  COUNTER-CLOCKWISE    lerp_angle(0, PI + 8 * TAU, 0.5) = -1.570796
i=9  CLOCKWISE            lerp_angle(0, PI + 9 * TAU, 0.5) =  1.570796
```

Okay, removing `color /= 1.0 - dot(color.rgb, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114));` and changing the luminance calculation back to what it was results in the mobile renderer blur to be much brighter then the clustered one. A reverse of the previous situation.

However putting it back in the size of the blur become nearly identical with the same intensity values. The problem however is that the mobile renderer is again starting to max out on the glow buffers because you really need to crank up the strength of the glow to get a nice blur and we're hitting max values in the glow buffers themselves now.

Also both with the clustered and mobile renderer, it seems like blue is nearly filtered out, not surprising seeing the values we're doing the dot product with.

I don't know enough about the proper color calculations needed here but Clayjohns remark that the colors aren't tone mapped is spot on, tonemapping doesn't happen until after the glow buffers have been created and applied in the tonemap shader. I'm feeling that what the clustered renderer is doing is actually wrong...

I'm keeping the tonemapping thing in both shaders for now so they are atleast similar in result, however I think this needs more debate (also posted this in `#rendering`)

I think "finalize" as proposed in your poll might be a better term. "uninitialize" might be a bit more common than "deinitialize" but it's also used for _uninitialized variable_, which means something which _has not been initialized yet_. While here things have been initialized, used, and now need to be cleaned up (which is usually different from just de-initializing variables).

Actually as I write this, "deinitialize" sounds a bit better to avoid the confusion with _not yet initialized_ "uninitialized". That is if we want to keep "initialize" as part of the name since the enums are about `INITIALIZATION_LEVEL`. Otherwise I think another term like "finalize" can be clearer and less prone to typos (it's always super difficult to spell uninitialize IMO with all those ni's :P).

Alternatively, I like "cleanup" too for this kind of task.

Sorry this is a bit of a mess - it turns out the checks were unnecessary (and didn't do anything) anyway, since the text has already been passed through `rstize_text`. When being edited by `indent_bullets`, the codeblocks will have been converted to rst:

```
::

    codeblock text here
    - leading bullet point characters will be fine
```

where the text is [always indented with spaces, not tabs](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/community/contributing/class_reference_writing_guidelines.html#):

> Use [codeblock] for pre-formatted code blocks. Inside [codeblock], always use four spaces for indentation. The parser will delete tabs. 

and the text on any non-empty line is [preceded by at least four spaces](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/61517b6d3994f419580a89f5ba3270681c442dd6/doc/tools/make_rst.py#L892). `indent_bullets` will see that the first character after any leading tabs is a space, not a bullet point character, and so skip over the line.

I've taken the codeblock checks back out again.

body:
Since there are no project settings for this, there doesn't seem to be a way to change the VRS mode on the root Viewport without using a script or a custom viewport. This should probably be added by allowing the user to specify the mode for the root Viewport, and a texture path. If changing the mode to XR doesn't make sense for the root Viewport, then the option should be hidden and only Disabled and Texture should be displayed.

The documentation should also mention what format is expected for `vrs_texture`:

- Which color format should the image have? I assume it's `Image.FORMAT_RGB8`, but this should be mentioned explicitly, especially if other modes don't work.
- Which colors should be used to represent individual shading rates?
- What resolution should the texture be? Can it have a different resolution or aspect ratio than the viewport?
- What happens if a texture with invalid colors is used? Is the nearest color used instead, or is an error printed? (If not, there should probably be some kind of validation in debug builds. In any case, the "invalid" behavior should be documented.)

___

Also, I think a global VRS override should be supported for performance testing purposes. While this is generally not meant for use in production, it can be used to see how much performance you could gain from enabling VRS in theory.

This could be a list of premade textures with all pixels set to 1×2, 2×1, 2×2 and so on. This would also be good to expose as a VRS mode in the project settings. This can be done in a future PR though – I'll open a proposal in that case, so we remember to do it in the future.
author: Calinou

body:
I think the biggest issue especially with VRS on XR is that you generally don't want to turn it on until it is available. With non-XR use cases the texture may not be available from the start especially if the texture is not a fixed texture but one generated (at the moment only possible for code, but we should investigate some day creating viewports based on different texture formats including R8_NORM

It's also very likely that you wouldn't turn VRS on in a menu screen, but do turn it on in the main viewport when your game actually starts (especially in non-XR use cases), that likely will only be a feasible option to do in code.

That all said, out of principle having these settings available as project settings, even if only to make it clear this functionality is supported on the main viewport, and for making it easier to run test projects, yeah it may not be a bad idea to just add them and accept they have limited uses.

body:
> In particular, I had to specify a default capture mode to get it to compile for some parts that were using GLOBAL_GET.

You can pass `SETTING_NAME` in as a parameter to avoid capturing anything.

```suggestion
#define GLOBAL_GET_FAST(VAR_TYPE, SETTING_NAME) ([](const StringName &p_name) -> const VAR_TYPE & {\
	static VAR_TYPE local_var;                                                   \
		static uint32_t local_version = 0;                                      \
		uint32_t new_version = ProjectSettings::get_singleton()->get_version(); \
		if (local_version != new_version) {                                     \
			local_version = new_version;                                        \
			local_var = ProjectSettings::get_singleton()->get(p_name);     \
		}					                                                   \
		return local_var; })(SETTING_NAME)
```

Also maybe this macro should be `GLOBAL_GET_CACHED` since `GLOBAL_GET_UNCACHED` is used?
author: timothyqiu

body:
Ah excellent I'll try that with the parameter. :+1: 

On the naming, I'm open to suggestions. When I talked with @akien-mga  earlier we were going with the idea of replacing the existing `GLOBAL_GET` wholesale for most cases, so no changes to existing code were needed. The uncached version I added for "backward" support, but it isn't used anywhere so could potentially be removed.

So that mainly leaves what to call the `FAST` version. I did think about `GLOBAL_GET_CACHED` but, both are cached now, so the only difference is that this version stores a type instead of a variant. It could be called e.g. `GLOBAL_GET_TYPED`, but then that isn't very clear from the use areas _why_ it might be used in preference to `GLOBAL_GET`. But I'm welcoming any ideas here.

In the incident, that the node gets reparented to another node when its owner has its editable status removed, it may conflict with a matching name. By storing the names in an array, it means it can correctly restore its original name upon undoing.
author: SaracenOne

body:
While it seems overkill, I can explain why we have the names and transforms array. For explanation of names, see the explanation to the above response about undoing naming conflicts. As for the transforms, while its uncommon given a revert chain should put things back to its relative position before the reparent, storing the original transforms will restore it in situations where the local position might change. In example I was testing, I had a scene with an animated skeleton and bone attachments. If I instance this scene in another scene, make it editable, then attach a mesh to that bone attachment, then remove the editable status, the mesh will become detached. This is fine, but if the skeleton is animating, upon undoing the action to remove the editable children status, we don't know how to restore it local position by just using reparenting, hence the use of the transform array.

Admittedly, yeah, it this wasn't doing anything because the code to restore the local transform got lost during the migration to the reparent function, but I've restored it now.

> I could not leave it, because it causes the popup to get pushed off screen. However, I also could not fix it, because it isn't clear what it is trying to do. There is a comment that it is trying to put the popup within the bounds of the graph.
>
> I can't figure out why this would have been a requirement? Surely if the main window is currently small on the screen, you don't want the popup to try to fit inside it? It is a floating window.

You have to remember that Godot before 4.0 did not support multiple windows. So all dialogs were embedded in the main window (which can be reproduced in 4.0 by enabling single window mode).

So this code probably tries to make sure that the dialog in 3.x and in single window mode in 4.0 fits within the bounds of the graph editor. Since windowing changed in 4.0, this may no longer be needed, or may indeed be done wrong. So it can either be removed completely if the issue it tries to solve is no longer an issue, or fixed.

I'd suggest removing, after checking how things work in Single Window Mode.

body:
With the above approach, it is possible the user will ask navigation mesh to bake on the thread but Godot will silently do it off thread. IMHO that's wrong. As a user, in the situation when I `bake(true)` and the platform does not support threading, I'd expect a warning (in case of fallback to off-thread baking) or error (in case we block such scenario entirely).

I guess lots of users used to not care about warnings, so a warning about auto fallback may be overlooked - yet it may have a severe impact on performance. Therefore I'd say we should issue an error asking one to not use `on_thread=true` in such case.

body:
For "parseable" vs "parsable", both uses seem valid but the latter seems recommended: https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/parsable

```suggestion
		Navigation mesh baking happens in multiple steps and the result depends on 3D source geometry and properties of the [NavigationMesh] resource. In the first step, starting from a root node and depending on [NavigationMesh] properties all valid 3D source geometry nodes are collected from the [SceneTree]. Second, all collected nodes are parsed for their relevant 3D geometry data and a combined 3D mesh is build. Due to the many different types of parsable objects, from normal [MeshInstance3D]s to [CSGShape3D]s or various [CollisionObject3D]s, some operations to collect geometry data can trigger [RenderingServer] and [PhysicsServer3D] synchronizations. Server synchronization can have a negative effect on baking time or framerate as it often involves [Mutex] locking for thread security. Many parsable objects and the continuous synchronization with other threaded Servers can increase the baking time significantly. On the other hand only a few but very large and complex objects will take some time to prepare for the Servers which can noticeably stall the next frame render. As a general rule the total amount of parsable objects and their individual size and complexity should be balanced to avoid framerate issues or very long baking times. The combined mesh is then passed to the Recast Navigation Object to test the source geometry for walkable terrain suitable to [NavigationMesh] agent properties by creating a voxel world around the meshes bounding area.
```

Sorry for not looking at this sooner. It does look like this is improving issues that the SkeletonModificaitonStack two-bone IK solver has. It seems way less inclined to freak out now. However, it's unclear if the intention was to solve situations where you might have a bone chain with non-uniform rolls, since that still appears to break the IK and cause mangling. Whatever the case, it does seem to be an improvement over the old implementation at least which was seemed very broken.

However, more importantly, it is worth noting that while this improves two-bone IK, it also appears to have caused regressions in the FABRIK IK solvers, both the newer skeleton modifier stack implementation (which completely freaks out now), and the old SkeletonIK3D node (which seems to behave consistently now regardless of bone rolls but is otherwise mangled. This one may end up being deprecated in the future, but I still don't think it should be knowingly broken). It looks like the other comments did mention FABRIK and how since this PR doesn't touch it directly, I'm guessing the changes to the rotate_to_align function must have caused the regression.

I've attached a sample project which demonstrates comparisons of some IK solvers to demonstrate the issues I described.

body:
> Can the signal not come from the particle system, rather than the particle?

This is already what happens, but the issue is passing the data to the signal in a way that is compatible with the scripting API. GDScript does not have a `struct` type, so type-safe data must be passed via custom objects.

We could emit an array of dictionaries in the signal, but it's not strongly typed. This means there's no autocompletion and errors will only occur at run-time in scripts (instead of compile-time). Parts of the Godot API use dictionaries for that reason, but I feel this is something that should be avoided in the long run.

body:
I'm not sure that this addresses the use-case in https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/3013

This change may be helpful as it allows users to control where the blend starts and thus may help with some edge cases, but ultimately, the problem will still exist. Take for example, the example in the OP. With this change, the user could tweak the blend start so that very little light leaked into the room, by setting the fade start at roughly the room extents. The issue is this just pushes the blend portion outside of the room, so you will end up with occlusion artifacts outside of the room. What is needed is for us to save a depth map with the reflection probe and then use the depth map to blend.

body:
Great work! You are getting much closer to a working implementation. 

Now is the time for us to solidify exactly what the API should look like as I can see you and I have differing ideas. 

My thinking was to just expose two booleans ``keep_3d_linear`` (2D is always sRGB), and ``force_high_precision``. 

``keep_3d_linear`` would be assigned to the render_target and would disable linear->sRGB in the tonemapper. You have this nearly implemented now and it should be fine. 

For ``force_high_precision`` my idea was that it would also get assigned to the render_target and then during allocation, the rendertarget would select between two formats based on what ``force_high_precision`` is set to. 

In my opinion, the above is about as simple as we can make this feature (it also worked similarly in 3.x).

However, I can see you are going in a slightly different direction, one which would provide the user with a little more flexibility by allowing them to override the default precision. I like this idea as well, and it aligns with our goal of giving users more control in 4.0. 

Accordingly, if you want to expose the ability to set the color format directly I would do it as follows:
1. Still have ``keep_3d_linear`` (this is needed in any case)
2. do not create ``force_high_precision`` instead create an ``override_color_format`` variable in Viewport which would call ``render_target_set_override_color_format`` (the same as your current ``render_target_set_color_format``). Then in ``update_render_target`` you check and see if ``override_color_format`` is used, if it is, then you set ``color_format``, ``color_format_srgb``, and ``image_format`` based on ``override_color_format``, if not, you just use the default.

Mobile devices don't typically support RGBA16 or RGB16 (some do through extensions though). So we can't rely on support being available. We will have to add a config setting ``framebuffer_half_float_supported`` and then fall back to low precision if it is false. You can initialize the config the same way we do in 3.x, e.g. in storage/config.cpp:
```
#ifdef GLES_OVER_GL
	config.framebuffer_float_supported = true;
#else
	framebuffer_float_supported = config.extensions.has("GL_EXT_color_buffer_float");
#endif

No rendering books were harmed in the making of this dither jittering algorithm :slightly_smiling_face: 

On a more serious note, this is the same algorithm I used in my initial proof of concept (before TAA was merged). Any ideas for "proper" but cheap jittering patterns that could provide better results?
author: Calinou

body:
The way the current per-pixel rotation works is actually already optimized to work with TAA. What you want to do is instead increase r (the rotation amount) by the proportion of the TAA cycle you are in e.g. TAA_FRAME/NUMBER_OF_JITTERS. So if you use 16 different jittered samples, you would use ``(frame %16)/16``. Then, add it to the result of quick_hash before multiplying by TAU. 

Remember ``r`` represents a rotation of the Vogel disk. It is not a dither. We rotate the Vogel disk randomly per pixel to break up patterns, but we also want to rotate it over time. 

The beauty of the Vogel disk is that, when rotated, the path created by each sample will not overlap the path from another. So by using a rotation, you are able to spread the samples out and maximize the benefit of the TAA

body:
Testing this out locally I noticed that the temporal supersampling seemed to introduce some artifacts in the penumbra that weren't their before. So I returned to http://www.iryoku.com/next-generation-post-processing-in-call-of-duty-advanced-warfare to see what we are missing and noticed something interesting. The author suggests an approach for use with 2X SMAA, he says you should use ``IGN() * 0.5 + frame`` where frame flips between ``0.0`` and ``0.5``. I realized that as implemented the rotation ranges from ``0`` to ``4 * PI`` because both IGN and frame range between 0 and 1. This creates an issue where it is possible to sample the same (or essentially the same) rotation twice. Removing the ``2.0`` multiplier restores the range to ``0`` to `` 2 * PI`` and improves the result. 

One final optimization, since we are only using ``frame`` to calculate this rotation. And since we are using 32 bits anyway, we might as well pass ``frame`` as a float with ``JITTER_FRACTION`` baked in.

body:
There is a cost to the technique. If a parent has e.g. 1000 children, and only one is queued for deletion, then it will iterate through all the children _just in case_ any of them are queued. This could worst case result in a bunch of cache misses. So we ideally don't want to use it _unless_ we know it will help.

We know there is no possible benefit in using the optimization with a queue size of 1, and we know the benefits tend to scale approximately with `number of children being deleted / number of children` (on average, it depends on the exact deletion patterns), so it makes sense to turn it on at some overall queue size between 2 and 1000 (which was measured somewhat inaccurately as 1.3x faster earlier).

In the same way there is less absolute benefit possible in a parent that has few children, as the effect scales something like O(n*n) where n is the number of children.

The magic numbers in both cases could probably be decreased (maybe as a result of further testing), but this conservative approach should be good to start because it will eliminate most long pauses.

There are a few more complex techniques which could be used to achieve the same thing in a less "haphazard" fashion, such as sorting the queue delete list, or having a list of queue deleted nodes on each node, but the main difficulty is that currently each node has no idea of its child ID relative to its parent. This could be fixed by storing a child ID per node and keeping it up to date as children are added / moved, but it is pretty easy for bugs to creep in here and for it to get out of sync. So the simple approach in this PR is probably more sensible to get started (unless profiling shows the same thing is a problem in other situations).

Another variation is we could store a counter of the number of queue deleted children per node, and use this as a heuristic "number in queue / number of children" to turn on or off.

body:
The beauty of this hash function is that it is a general purpose hash function that just works on any form of data. As it is already done with several types in this PR, you can pass any type together with its size in bytes to it. For example Vector2i: `hash_murmur3_32_buffer(&p_vec, sizeof(Vector2i));`
I had dedicated versions for primitive types, but they didn't provide any performance benefit compared to this general variant. Nearly all places where dbj2 is used can be easily replaced with this buffer version. (However, at one point, I had replaced the dbj2 string hash functions (in ustring.cpp) with murmur3 but that broke ClassDB for some reason and I have no clue why).

Besides that, I am not sure if the quality of murmur3 will still be the same if I modify it to work like the dbj2 hash functions (because that is not how it was intended to be used and hash functions are quite fragile). I could do some tests, but that might take some time.
For now I added a seed parameter which defaults to the same random prime number as before.

body:
I prefer to still enforce setting ``last_custom_format`` before setting the first vertex as it allows us to warn users when they are setting custom data without setting a format. 

With these changes, it is entirely possible that users will call ``set_custom`` but never call call ``set_custom_format`` in which case the custom data will be silently ignored. By forcing users to ``set_custom_format`` before adding data, we can ensure that they actually set the custom format. 

I don't see a reason why it is helpful for users to set the custom format after setting all the data anyway. In practice, you need to know your custom format before setting the data anyway, so requiring ``set_custom_format`` before the first call to ``set_vertex`` is not a big deal.

```suggestion
				Returns the value of the setting identified by [param name]. If the setting doesn't exist and [param default_value] is specified, the value of [param default_value] is returned. Otherwise, [code]null[/code] is returned.
```

You shouldn't use a line break like that in the XML docs. A line break adds a new paragraph, which is excessive for such short lines.

You should also use `[param foo]` to refer to method parameters in text, which allows it to be highlighted better, builds cognitive connection between the method signature and the description, and makes the job of translators easier when adapting the docs to another language. And it is also validated on the CI so you don't make typos, as a bonus.

For the description itself, I don't think it's correct to refer to this as "setting" a default value. You aren't setting it, you provide it as a fallback.

body:
Source: https://bottosson.github.io/posts/colorpicker/

> Picking colors is a common operation in many applications and over the years color pickers have become fairly standardized. Ubiquitous today are color pickers based on [HSL and HSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSL_and_HSV). They are simple transformations of RGB values to alternative coordinates chosen to better correlate with perceptual qualities.

> Despite color picking playing a big role in a lot of applications, the design of color pickers isn’t a particularly well researched topic. While some variation exist in the widgets themselves, the choice of HSL or HSV is mostly taken for granted, with only a few exceptions.

> By far the most used color spaces today for color picking are [HSL and HSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSL_and_HSV), two representations introduced in the classic 1978 paper [“Color Spaces for Computer Graphics”](https://doi.org/10.1145/800248.807362). HSL and HSV designed to roughly correlate with perceptual color properties while being very simple and cheap to compute.

> Worth noting is that HSL and HSV are not quite color spaces on their own, they are transformations from a source RGB color space. For each set of RGB primaries and transfer functions, the transformation to HSL and HSV produces unique color spaces. Today HSL and HSV are most commonly used together with the sRGB color space, so that is what we will look at here and we will here use HSL and HSV to refer to HSL and HSV for the sRGB color space.

> Also useful to note is that HSL and HSV are not continuously differentiable, so that limits their use with numerical optimization and machine learning.

> One of the main advantages of HSL and HSV over the different Lab color spaces is that they map the sRGB gamut to a cylinder. This makes them easy to use since all parameters can be changed independently, without the risk of creating colors outside of the target gamut.

> We will attempt to do just that by creating new color spaces similar to HSL and HSV but that better match perception. This will be done by leveraging the Oklab color space. Using Oklab here over more advanced models such as CAM16 is useful because working out the math becomes a lot simpler. It also means that it won’t be a full color model able to adapt to different viewing conditions, but that is probably also desirable here since it is more practical.

> For consistency with the naming of Oklab, these new color spaces will be called Okhsl and Okhsv. The parameters will also be referred to as hhh, sss and lll and hhh, sss and vvv respectively. Those names are a bit confusing but I think making the new spaces easy to adopt for someone used to HSL and HSV is more important than trying to establish new names.

body:
This PR indirectly limits the size:

1. Make `min_size` and `max_size` follow the size limit of the rendering server, see `Window::_clamp_limit_size()`;
2. Then make sure that `max_size_used` is not less than `min_size`, see `Window::_validate_limit_size()`.

`max_size_used` is the upper limit of actual use, it will be clamped by `min_size` and `max_size`, combined with 1, it will eventually follow the size limit of the rendering server.

`get_clamped_minimum_size()` returns the actual lower bound used, which takes into account the case when `wrap_controls` is enabled.

body:
While I believe that it would clearly make more *sense* for an `is_class` method to return the name of the best understood typename, as you have implemented, I also believe that modifying this method in this manner is too dangerous. `is_class()` is used frequently throughout the engine with the assumption that the returned class name will correspond to an actual natively-implemented class stored in the `ClassDB`. This makes it still work properly and be applicable for extensions, but not so for scripted types.

Rather than this sort of solution, I would *much* prefer to see something where we add an entirely different method to the base class that handles abstracting away the complexity of the script class name vs. the native class name. In which case, we should decide on the name of that method in the related Issue (#21789) probably. Other than that though, I like a lot of the modifications you've made, personally.

This also goes for the `is_class` method definition in the object macro further up in this same file.

author: willnationsdev

body:
> I'm confused as to why adding the Script type checking to is_class could be a bad thing

I think I initially confused this with `get_class()` for some reason which is used pretty extensively in the engine source code. I don't know how often `is_class()` is used, but if it's a lot less then *maybe* it would be less problematic? Still would end up adding to the inconsistency vs. the similarly named `get_class()` though.

It's less so that it's a "bad thing" if you added this functionality, but more so that you'd need to double check every reference to this method in the rest of the codebase to ensure it's logic is still consistent should the value return `true` unexpectedly. For example, if the code passed in a typename string to verify that the given typename is the name of an inherited *native* type when (cause it needs to verify it to do some native-only operation that is incompatible with scripted types), then making this change would suddenly make it possible for previously unsupported - and correctly incompatible - types to now slip through that check. That's the "risk". We would need to ensure that things that use this method to control flow logic don't e.g. do anything with the `ClassDB` since those operations would surely fail and/or log an error after this change is made.

> why a separate method would be required?

If a separate method is defined instead, then it means no one would have to do the above "cleanup" refactoring/investigating throughout the rest of the codebase after the change is made. BUT, I do agree that it could lead to redundancy / choice paralysis or confusion regarding which method should be used in which circumstances (a reoccurring source of confusion in Godot's API for newbies imo). So, it's not that it would be required. Just that IF we made the change, we'd need a corresponding correctional sweep of the rest of the codebase to go alongside it.

If Godot supports 16k textures (16384 x 16384), this may signed-integer-overflow in the event that the raw texture is over 2GB of VRAM and the texture is RGBAH *8 bytes per pixel) or RGBAF (16 bytes per pixel) format:
```
>>> 16384*16384*8
2147483648
>>> 16384*16384*16
4294967296
```

That said, I wouldn't expect such large textures to work particularly well on any hardware due to fragmentation, but thought it would be worth a comment.

body:
I had a look at the code and it looks like the PR works as advertised. Also the editor seems to work without problems from a few quick tests.
From what I can tell, the behavior doesn't change, if the newly introduced functionality (focus layers) isn't used, so it stays compatible to current behavior. However it changes the API of two functions that are exposed to GDScript.

Since #79480 tries to accomplish the same goal in a different way, I want to include a comparison of the two PRs. Both have advantages and disadvantages, so it is difficult for me to tell, which of the two approaches would be better suited.

| Topic | This PR | #79480 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Size of change | +176 −64 | +17 −10 |
| Behavior change | no, current behavior stays the same, only adds functionality | method for focusing Controls is redefined and becomes more complex |
| Chance of introducing regressions | low | medium to high |
| API change | `gui_get_focus_owner` and `gui_release_focus` change their GDScript API signature | no API change |
| Maintenance | the concept of focus layers adds complexity to Viewports and Controls | no additional concepts are introduced |
| Performance | should have no to little impact | Every group of linked Controls requires a separate SubViewport. Additional Viewports have a negative impact on rendering performance |
| Screen space real estate | Adds focus_layer to Control inspector | no changes to inspector |
| Discoverability | focus layer is introduced as new variable in the inspector, so it can be discovered easily | Can only be discovered when multiple SubViewports are used, so the functionality can be considered difficult to discover |

body:
This change broke Gradient's cubic interpolation mode. The first and last points use a solid color and the middle points have some kind of an off-by-one error. I tried to fix this myself but only made it worse :/

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/67974470/179372293-81218b37-7639-496a-a6ed-c9e706d053ef.png)

If it helps, I took the `cubic_interpolate()` method in `Gradient.h` that was removed in this commit and compared it to `Math::cubic_interpolate()` to pinpoint the difference. Since the arguments have different names in both functions, I replaced the first 4 with `A` `B` `C` and `D` and the fifth with `weight`. Comparing them this way made me see that the functions are not the same.

```cpp
Math::cubic_interpolate()
0.5 * ((A * 2.0) + (-C + B) * weight + (2.0 * C - 5.0 * A + 4.0 * B - D) * (weight * weight) + (-C + 3.0 * A - 3.0 * B + D) * (weight * weight * weight));

Gradient.h cubic_interpolate()
B + 0.5 * weight * (C - A + weight * (2.0 * A - 5.0 * B + 4.0 * C - D + weight * (3.0 * (B - C) + D - A)));
```

body:
Should be fine as `dest[0]` won't be evaluated [as an expression in `sizeof`](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/expressions#Unevaluated_expressions). It will only be deduced at the compile-time what the return type of `dest[0]` is. And currently it will deduce it's `int32_t` because that's what this operator returns:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f6072c9c98f11797e31a2076d17b580a6c651679/core/variant/variant_call.cpp#L755
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f6072c9c98f11797e31a2076d17b580a6c651679/core/variant/variant.h#L65
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f6072c9c98f11797e31a2076d17b580a6c651679/core/templates/vector.h#L92
author: kleonc

body:
Resizing can fail, it returns an `Error` which could be checked. Since here `dest` is being enlarged I think resizing can only fail in out of memory case. As far as I've checked `resize` will either succeed and resize to the given size or it will fail and leave the previous size unchanged. So here if `dest.resize()` will fail then it would produce an error and `dest.size()` will remain 0. Meaning if `size` was used it would try to `memcpy` to the memory being out of bounds of `dest`'s allocated memory. Using `dest.size()` prevents this, it's a good change.
I think the question is whether the error of `dest.resize()` should be checked explicitly instead (before `memcpy` is called).

body:
Not directly linked to this PR but noting it down as I review the code, this doesn't need to use `TTRC` here + `TTRGET` in `_create_member_item`. Instead it could use `TTR()` here directly and just use the translated `p_type` in `_create_member_item`.

`TTRC` is used for cases where we don't want to string translated automatically, but it's just a marker for our strings extractor to get the source string - which is then translated at runtime with `TTRGET`. While `TTR` just does the translation in place, which seems suitable here (I don't see code that expects `p_type` to be the original English string).

> I'll try and get this fixed today

Well that was a long day 🙃, thanks for your patience

So the problem was from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/64271. Adding an error message to the log requires access to its theme items (e.g. error icon). https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/060d0ce88204f9180beb3764048975e9dcf5c496/modules/gltf/register_types.cpp#L99 is getting called before the EditorLog has entered the SceneTree. This means `NOTIFICATION_THEME_CHANGED` won't have been called yet, and the EditorLog's theme cache won't have been initialized, hence the crash. Fortunately, the log is already rebuilt anyway  on `NOTIFICATION_THEME_CHANGE`, so I added this check to simply `return` early if the EditorLog hasn't entered the scene yet. Theoretically this should be more performant anyway since it won't have to add the log line twice.

Part of the issue here is that that global shader uniforms hashmap takes any RID. I.e. it doesn't check if the RID is for a geometry instance. I think you will need to store a ``->self`` value in ``RenderGeometryInstanceBase`` so you can access the RID of the GeometryInstance itself

			Scales the 3D render buffer based on the viewport size uses an image filter specified in [member rendering/scaling_3d/mode] to scale the output image to the full viewport size. Values lower than [code]1.0[/code] can be used to speed up 3D rendering at the cost of quality (undersampling). Accordingly, I would put the resolve inside of ``render_target_copy_to_back_buffer()``. If copying the full rect, you can get away with resolving the Multisampled buffer directly into the backbuffer. If copying a partial rect, you'll have to resolve and then copy still.

Shouldn't MSAA work on the edges of sprites with opaque borders (at least if they're rotated)? Sprites are rects after all, and they're probably drawn with 2 triangles behind the scenes.

To avoid confusion, what I'd mention instead is that MSAA will not smooth out nearest-neighbor filtered textures, as well as shader-induced aliasing. Currently combined 2D and 3D rendering is broken since the resolve attachment's store op is `VK_ATTACHMENT_STORE_OP_DONT_CARE` while it should be `VK_ATTACHMENT_STORE_OP_STORE`. (this took way too long to figure out :)) 
![grafik](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50084500/181396214-0f0a0ad1-e133-4d59-ab2c-bb657def724e.png)
Just brute forcing all store ops to `VK_ATTACHMENT_STORE_OP_STORE` resolves the issue:
![grafik](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50084500/181395672-4c1893d6-2284-46ef-b13c-7e8eec448bed.png)
Now that I know what's wrong I can work on a proper fix, will probably push one tomorrow after I addressed clayjohns review comments. (I also rewrote a few bits to make things cleaner)

Correct, the user data folder is in an app-private directory provided by [`Context.getFilesDir()`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/content/Context#getFilesDir()) that's not accessible to file manager.

> This method checks if export templates are valid. If they're not valid on PC, it should behave the same as if they're not valid on Android. With this change it will be true on Android and false on PC, and the latter seems more accurate to me.

The method unfortunately is a catch-all for export templates validity checks, and project configuration validity checks.
For a full binary export, both checks are valid. However for a `pck/zip` only export, the export templates validity checks are irrelevant.
So given we'll only (initially) support `pck/zip` export for the Android editor, the export templates validity checks are being disabled. So yes in this scenario, if the project configuration validity checks fail, they fail both on Android and Windows. If the export templates validity checks fail, they only fail on Windows but not on Android.

> Which is partially true at least for Mono (BCL needs to be included in the PCK), but can also not be a deal-breaker for simple projects.

The flow I'm imagining is that a user would do development and testing using the Android editor port, then via export of a zip or pck file, remote versioning or file syncing, continue and finish the release process on a fully featured platform. Would the BCL need to be included for that workflow to work?

 >  Or if a temporary hack is needed for Android, it can simply be not to call can_export since your changes basically makes it a no-op.

The `can_export` call is still needed for the project configuration validity checks. This particular method is overwritten by the `EditorExportPlatformWindows::can_export` method which uses this parent logic for its template validation logic, so the short-circuit for Android is still needed.

> So what's needed IMO is a bigger refactor that decouples PCK export check from binary export check.

Agree this would be a good approach as well. Splitting `can_export` into a `validate_export_templates` and a `validate_project_configuration` methods. We can then skip the call to the `validate_export_templates` for the Android editor.

body:
The optimization comment is regarding using WaitForMultipleObjects (Windows) or similar primitives that allow you to blocking wait on both task_available_semaphore and done_semaphore at the same time.  That allows the thread to not busy wait and give up the CPU via microsleeping, and instead actually get descheduled exactly until the wait completes.

A Linux equivalent (ancient) would be poll against multiple eventfd.  Not sure what the modern equivalent of that is.
author: derammo

body:
This will need careful user documentation.  There may be user task code on the stack, as tasks can wait on other tasks.  User task code must be fully re-entrant for this to not lead to self-deadlock on the user side. 

For example, Task X's task function includes submitting Task Y and then waiting on it.   Without the body of Task X going off the stack, this wait can execute Task Z on the same thread.  That may be the same function as Task X or another one.   Either way, the user must understand they can't hold locks or have any "incomplete" shared state when they call "wait_for_task_completion."   It is a great simplification to avoid deadlock on the worker thread side, but it will need careful usage from the user.
author: derammo

body: This isn't really an error.   It should be possible to submit a bunch of long running tasks and then exit the program.  For that to work, you'd need an additional (optional) Callable in add_task(...) so that there is a separate function to call for cancellation.   At shut down, all pending tasks get called on the cancellation callback.  Waiting on a task that was canceled must then also survive without error, because some of the user code may at the same time call wait_for_task_completion(...) during the shutdown process, based on timing.   If ThreadRunner was RefCounted, you could probably just keep all the task objects that were canceled, with the semaphores posted.   Then these deallocate only when all customers of the ThreadRunner are gone.

In the normal case, you check this atomic, and it is false.  Then you call _process_task() which 100% of the time grabs the mutex.   In all cases except on exit, the atomic access isn't useful and is just another synchronization point.

body:
More context in case it is useful:

An async API should always have a guarantee of _exactly_ one callback.   This is so that user code can allocate stuff for the async request, stick it in user data, and clean it up on callback.   When the system shuts down, this state needs to be cleaned up, but it may not be possible to execute the queued work, because the system is going down.  

Additionally, it is just slow to have shut down wait for a bunch of work that nobody is going to use anyway.  That's why there normally is a callback parameter that tells you if you are supposed to just clean up or actually do your work, or you can have an additional callback (Callable) to call if the work item / task gets canceled before running.  Because you can't force GD clients to have a particular callback signature, I think the optional Callable is the better way here.  In that case, the guarantee will be that either your work function gets called or the cancellation callback.  Either way, you know you can clean up whatever related stuff you may have.

> I don't know why it's tested this way either, I wonder if the test is not weak, for example if there's diagonal 2 0 1, this test might detect it as an identity matrix `(Math::abs(rows[0][0] + rows[1][1] + rows[2][2] - 3) < angle_epsilon`

@fabriceci Not gonna lie, I haven't noticed this last condition before. :laughing: And yeah, it looks absolutely incorrect.

> I just wonder if the first condition (just before the identity one) can be replaced by `is_diagonal` and then we can skip the diagonal test and only check for the 1.

@fabriceci The first condition is meant to check whether the matrix is [singular](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SingularMatrix.html), not whether it's [diagonal](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DiagonalMatrix.html). So no, the first check can't be replaced by `is_diagonal` call.

However, the current check for singularity seems strange/incomplete? :thinking: I mean matrix can be singular / not invertable if this condition isn't met, trivial example:
```
0 0 0
1 2 3
4 5 6
```
So I guess the question is whether there are some assumptions about the actual matrix of the `Basis`. Maybe such matrix is assumed to be invalid / it's assumed to be impossible to obtain such data in `Basis`. But if there are no restrictions then this check would need to be broader. In theory a check for determinant being zero should be sufficient.

body:
I think the new approach is too close to something we already have with `EditorData::add_move_array_element_function` and `EditorInspectorArray::setup_with_move_element_function`, covering the exact same use case but from the object directly instead of an editor plugin.

I think this PR is incomplete and needs few changes:
- Remove EditorData::add_move_array_element_function, and replace it with the new approach where it is used.
- The moving/adding/removing function (here add and swap) should be arguments of `EditorInspectorArray::setup_with_move_element_function`, as that is what this function was built for.

On a side note, I don't like much having to provide a swap function. Having only a swapping function will mean that it will have to be called a lot when you would need to move an element from one place to another. Depending on the underlying structure used to store the array, this can have a significant performance impact, especially when you are using Vector and/or need to update some side data structure (like a cache for example, or something like that). This is particularly the case for TileSet data layers for example.
Instead, the function should required to be called only once for each operation you need to do, so that those sort of underlying updates can be only triggered once per operation.

So what I suggest instead is to replace the `swap` function by a `move` function, so instead of swapping two elements, it takes one element and move it to another position. We can keep the same logic for `p_element_index < 0` and `p_to_pos < 0` to respectively to add and remove elements. This should avoid any performance issue.

body:
It is indeed somewhat arbitrary but this should be the default install path for a distro-packaged mold.

We can't use `which mold` as this gives `/usr/bin/mold`, but for the `-B` linker option GCC expects a path to a folder with a file named `ld` (yes that's software designed in the 90s...):
```
$ ls -l /usr/libexec/mold/
total 0
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 14 Jul  1 10:45 ld -> ../../bin/mold*
```

Expand "A classic way to use mold" in https://github.com/rui314/mold#how-to-use for details.

Possible install locations for this would be:
- `/usr/libexec/mold` if using `PREFIX=/usr`, which is what most Linux distros would do when packaging
- `/usr/local/libexec/mold` if using `PREFIX=/usr/local`, which is the default and hence what users who self-install mold from source might have
- Any arbitrary location if users pass a different `PREFIX` or hack the `Makefile`

I chose to only support the distro package scenario as the rest is IMO too difficult to handle. We could maybe at least do a check that `/usr/libexec/mold/ld` or `/usr/local/libexec/mold/ld` exist and use it, or abort.

body:
I see why you did it, but I think that the idea was to force GCC's `ranlib` and `ar` just when LTOing since that's required by GCC for it.

From the gcc man page:
```
           If object files containing GIMPLE bytecode are stored in a library
           archive, say libfoo.a, it is possible to extract and use them in an
           LTO link if you are using a linker with plugin support.  To create
           static libraries suitable for LTO, use gcc-ar and gcc-ranlib
           instead of ar and ranlib; to show the symbols of object files with
           GIMPLE bytecode, use gcc-nm.  Those commands require that ar,
           ranlib and nm have been compiled with plugin support.  At link
           time, use the flag -fuse-linker-plugin to ensure that the library
           participates in the LTO optimization process:

                   gcc -o myprog -O2 -flto -fuse-linker-plugin a.o b.o -lfoo
```

body:
Done some testing with editor `release-debug` builds on ARM64 macOS, and do a comparison for the performance of opening large project in the editor, and stripped executable sizes:

| LTO       | Link time (real) | Link time (CPU time) | Memory used by linker | Executable size | Speed improvement |
|-----------|------------------|----------------------|-----------------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| No LTO    | < 1 min          | < 1 min              | ~ 500 MB              | 109 MB          | Reference         |
| Full LTO  | 2:30 h           | 1:20 h               | ~ 48 GB               | 120 MB          | ~ 1-2%            |
| Thin LTO  | 16 min           | 1:50 h               | ~ 6 GB                | 132 MB          | ~ 1%              |

Seems like LTO is almost entirely useless.

`check_for_rename_gdscript_functions` additionally prints exactly in which line change will happen.
At beginning it was very different than `rename_gdscript_functions`, but I unified this one day, so there is a lot of duplicated code, which could be extracted to another function, but when I tried to do it I failed due some strange Regex memory leaks(this shouldn't be too hard to fix)

sort_custom( a , b ) -> sort_custom(Callable( a , b ))

body:
It needs to traverse all the child controls to calculate it.

The main purpose of `ScrollContainer::update_scrollbars()` is to confirm the status (`max`/`page`/`visible`) of scrollbars, it needs the largest one of the minimum size of child controls (`child_max_size`) already have been determined.

`ScrollContainer::_update_dimensions()` mainly determines the `rect` of the child controls. The `rect` needs to be calculated according to the `value` of the `ScrollBar`s.

So in terms of dependencies, it is unlikely to calculate all the data in one loop. Two loops are required. 

For convenience, it is better to calculate in `get_minimum_size()`. As the containers call `update_minimum_size()` before calling `queue_sort()`. See `*_child_notify(Node *p_child)` in `Container`.

body:
A while since I did any enum binding, but do we need to bind a `MAX`?
Is it useful to users, and does it have any implications for when new values are added to the enum?

(Speaking as a user this was kind of confusing, as if metric MAX might give the max FPS rather than the max of the enum.)
author: lawnjelly

body:
> A while since I did any enum binding, but do we need to bind a `MAX`?

It's not a strict requirement, but we generally do it for exposed enums. It allows users to loop over the size of the enum or implement cycling logic without hardcoding the size of the enum, as there is no reflection in GDScript on C++ enums. Reflection is supported on GDScript enums though, since they're internally dictionaries.

```gdscript
for metric in range(Engine.FPS_METRIC_MAX):
	pass

# Or:
var fps_metric: Engine.FPSMetric = Engine.FPS_METRIC_AVERAGE

func _input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
	if event.is_action_pressed("ui_accept"):
	fps_metric = wrapi(fps_metric + 1, 0, Engine.FPS_METRIC_MAX)
```

> and does it have any implications for when new values are added to the enum?

No, we can safely change its value without breaking compatibility. It's one exception to enum value changes since we assume people are not relying on the `_MAX` value for anything else than looping/iteration.

> (Speaking as a user this was kind of confusing, as if metric MAX might give the max FPS rather than the max of the enum.)

When the time comes to add a maximum metric, it'll be `FPS_METRIC_MAXIMUM` to avoid a conflict, and will be listed before `FPS_METRIC_MAX` (since that one always remains at the end of the enum).

The problem is that its not on/off. There are two additional things to consider here:
1) when it is set to `XRMODE_DEFAULT` we need a value that is different in many places, when we're checking if we need to compile XR shaders, we check the shader setting, if we check whether OpenXR needs to be setup, its checking that value, we'll soon be adding whether OpenXR needs to be setup in the editor. 2) once I start on the editor I want to switch between two ways of setting up the editor, a mode where you're purely running the editor in VR (which is the only mode available on stand alone headsets) and a mode where you still have the normal desktop UI combined with the in headset UI.

That said, at the moment I am thinking of removing the XRMODE_MIXED and just switch the scenario based on whether you're running stand alone VR or PCVR.

body:
@akien-mga but that doesn't work because when XRMODE_DEFAULT is set, they check different switches.

OpenXRAPI checks whether OpenXR needs to be enabled (i.e. `GLOBAL_GET("xr/openxr/enabled")`, hate the need to have this one but seeing OpenXR needs to take ownership of Vulkan we are living with this PITA setting)
RenderingCompositor checks whether the XR shader setting is enabled (i.e. `GLOBAL_GET("xr/shaders/enabled")`)

And in the near future the editor will check:
- an editor specific setting that tells us if the editor should run in XR mode (likely `EDITOR_GET("xr/enabled")`)
- whether OpenXR needs to be enabled in the editor (likely `GLOBAL_GET("xr/openxr/editor_enabled")`, though I may change enabled into a mode).

Setting XRMODE_ON overrides all these settings and enables them all. XRMODE_OFF turns them all off.

Hence the need for this check to be implemented **differently** in all this situations.

body:
> Roger that, but why is this bad?

It's not bad, but in this case it's mostly a style thing. `const` is important for pointers, references, and non-POD structs. But for primitive type arguments, the compiler is restricted by ABI and there is pretty much nothing to optimize. And it's not critical information for the developers, whether it's changed or not does not affect anything.

body:
Tested locally on Linux and macOS, it works as expected. Code looks good to me.

On Linux, I can't really spot a noticeable difference in CPU utilization on my 9950X3D with a debug build of 3.x. It's pretty low already (it oscillates between 0% and 1.9%, likely because of filesystem scanning).

On macOS 15.5 on a M4 Max, CPU utilization when the editor is on an empty Script tab (and unfocused) drops from 4.8% to 3.5% with this PR. I didn't have time to do extended battery drain tests yet.

I like the "mute on focus loss" ability, since it's pretty common to see in games. This makes this PR address https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/3693 for 3.x.

Some feedback:

- Since we have both `set_enabled()` and `is_enabled()` in AudioServer, we can expose an `enabled` property that would use those setter/getter methods.

body:
memnew calls `new Obj`.
`instantiate` is a function of `RefCounted`.
`ref_counted = memnew(MyObject)` is not valid (would need to be `ref_counted = Ref<MyObject>(memnew(MyObject))`).
You can also see the implementation here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/core/object/ref_counted.h#L226

body:
Thanks!

> I assume the from_peer_id is meant to be the unique network id the sender of that packet was initialized with?

Yep!

> And am I correct in assuming the target_id/target_peer is what it uses to deliver it the right place locally? I think some further documentation here would be helpful to know how to use `set_target_peer()` in conjunction with this.

No, the target peer is the remote peer to deliver the packet to. We don't need to say which peer to deliver to in `deliver_rpc()` because it's "this peer" - the developer should have already ensured that the packet only arrived at a peer that was intended to receive it.

The `set_target_peer()` method should ONLY be called by Godot internally! Developers should NOT be calling it themselves.

Yep, I see the logic in treating screen picking as a singular event that happens when the mouse is clicked, and I see the need for displaying the currently hovered color to the user. It's just that IMO the purpose of the "sample" (i.e. the swatch that displays the old and current colors) is a bit ambivalent. Most of the time the color that is shown on the sample is actually chosen, and events are emitted, except for when using the screen picker where it changes to display a temporary color that isn't chosen.

body:
Ah hang on, the penny drops. You want to pass the `RD::TextureFormat` struct in its entirety? For some reason I had in my head that you wanted to change this to `Image::Format` or something similar that was already exposed to GDScript...

This would greatly bloat a lot of the code where we now have a single line solution but I can see the use case for having it. 

For now I've changed it so that we have a:
`RID create_texture_from_format(const StringName &p_context, const StringName &p_texture_name, const RD::TextureFormat &p_texture_format, RD::TextureView p_view = RD::TextureView(), bool p_unique = true);`
That takes a texture format struct as input.

But I've left:
`RID create_texture(const StringName &p_context, const StringName &p_texture_name, const RD::DataFormat p_data_format, const uint32_t p_usage_bits, const RD::TextureSamples p_texture_samples = RD::TEXTURE_SAMPLES_1, const Size2i p_size = Size2i(0, 0), const uint32_t p_layers = 0, const uint32_t p_mipmaps = 1, bool p_unique = true);`
in place and this is what is called in most places with most properties left to default.
Internally it builds the correct texture format and calls `create_texture_from_format`.

This gives us a best of both world solution, it keeps the API lean in 99% of the cases, and in the 1% where we need to define a specific texture format, we can do so.

body:
Constant values can be optimized by the JIT (see https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/54186#discussion_r661724474).

So the usual pattern I see when using `stackalloc` is:

```csharp
Span<byte> stackSpan = length <= threshold ?
	stackalloc byte[threshold] :
	new byte[length];
```

APIs that take `Span` usually don't care about the span being bigger than the content it needs to write so usually they'd return the amount of elements written and you can use that to slice it.

```csharp
int writtenBytes = WriteToMySpan(stackSpan);
return stackSpan.Slice(0, writtenBytes);
```

body:
Is this change still needed at all? This looks wrong and might break on Windows (and is unnecessary on Linux).

The be clear, the `file://` protocol is `file://` - two slashes. After that should come a valid URI.

On Linux a valid URI for an absolute path will start with `/` so it will indeed be `file:///home/akien/...` etc.
On Windows AFAIU a valid URI will start with `c:\\path\\to\\root` so it would become `file://c:\\path\\to\\root` which should be fine.
author: akien-mga

body:
@akien-mga The problem is that this `root_uri` is later matched against other paths coming from the LSP client, and if I understand @A-Lamia correctly, they are sent like this on Windows clients: `file:///c:/path/to/root`.

EDIT: Rearranged words
author: permelin

body:
If that is the case, I wonder if this wouldn't be the less error prone way to do this?
```C
#ifndef WINDOWS_ENABLED
		workspace->root_uri = "file://" + workspace->root;
#else
		workspace->root_uri = "file:///" + workspace->root;
#endif
```
It assumes that `workspace_root` is always absolute, which seems like a reasonably safe assumption? It also assumes that the LSP client and server are on the same OS.

There is also the risk that this path format is actually different on different LSP client implementation on Windows.
author: permelin

body:
Alright, reading https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File_URI_scheme it does seem indeed that the prefix will often be `file:///` because it should be `file://` + `host` + `/` + `path` and `host` can be empty to default to localhost.

So `file:///c:/path/to/root` is indeed valid. And reading that page I would actually expect a Linux absolute path to be `file:////path/to/file` or `file://localhost//path/to/file`, but I guess they made the root slash optional.

So this fix looks good indeed.

body:
@akien-mga yes it works well on windows, with out it it does not work because it's not loading any files, it's being replaced by the URI in the LSP buffer so when it gets to `get_file_path()` it's given a raw parameter from the buffer that looks like,

windows: `file:///c%3A/path/to/root/path/to/file.gd`
linux: `file:///path/to/root/path/to/file.gd`

when workspace->root_uri is being set on LSP initialization it is set correctly on linux but incorrectly on windows. 

linux: `file:// + workspace->root`  -> `file:///path/to/root` -- Correct
LSP:   `file:///path/to/root/path/to/file.gd`

on windows how ever we get

windows: `file:// + workspace->root`  -> `file://C:/path/to/root` -- Incorrect
LSP:         `file:///c%3A/path/to/root/path/to/file.gd`

The return Basis contains the forward, up, and side vector together. Or use the [frenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frenet%E2%80%93Serret_formulas) vocabulary
>T(foward) is the unit vector [tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_vector) to the curve, pointing in the direction of motion.
>N(side) is the [normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_vector) unit vector, the derivative of T with respect to the [arclength parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifiable_path) of the curve, divided by its length.
>B(up) is the binormal unit vector, the [cross product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_product) of T and N.

Basically I need to return three Vector3 here. If Basis is not a good way what do you propose?

This function is essential for **smooth** interpolation of vectors between two neighboring baked point. `sample_baked_up_vector` is actually implemented based on `_sample_baked_basis`. If you think the name is not informative, we can change it at will, as it is only an internal method.

body:
As I have said many times, rotation is meaningless to `Curve3D`.

Also, you are not understanding `sample_baked` correctly.

If you want to implement `sample_baked_basis()`, you need to cache the rotation in `Vector<Basis>`, just like `tilt`s and `up_vector`s are stored in array. Since your current code is performing procedural calculations for the rotation, so `sample_baked` does not make sense.

Also, baking when there are multiple `RotationMode`s means that a `Vector<Vector<Basis>>` with as many elements as there are `RotationMode`s is needed. Having this in `Curve3D` is too evil. Since nothing uses rotation calculated from `Curve3D` except `Path3D`, a large amount of cache should not be placed there. It makes other classes that use `Curve3D` behave more heavily.

---

First, you need to implement `baked_forward_vector_cache` and `sample_baked_forward_vector()` correctly, referring to the `baked_up_vector_cache` implementation.

Rotation is meaningless in `Curve3D`, so call `Curve3D::sample_baked_/up_vector/forward_vector/position()` in `Path3D` to create `Transform3D` such as `Path3D::get_transform(float p_interval, RotationMode p_ rotaiton_mode)`. Then, you can create rotations and transforms in `Path3D` as you wish. If necessary, you can make a cache `Vector<Transform3D>` within `Path3D`.

> Reconsideration

I am really glad we come to some consensus, as to allow `Curve3D` to be sampled without going through other layer is the raison d'être of this PR. I will try my best to follow through.

## What `Rotation` is?
I reviewed all our previous discussion, and feel when we use the word `rotation`, we have different things in mind. And that cause unnecessary confusion. To facilitate further discussion,  we need to clarify some terms.

To me `rotation` have two parts:

- The first part is the intrinsic `rotation frame`, like the Frenet(TNB) frame I mentioned before. This part is mathematically well defined, you **can't change it** without inventing new kind of mathematical concepts(like tangent, and binormal). In the following discussion, I will call it `rotation frame` or `frame`.
- The second part is the `artistic control`, like locking X, Y, Z axes, setting up or target directions, etc. This part can be **changed by the user at will**. For example with `RotationMode` parameter.

## Where are we now?
> However, enum RotationMode should not be defined in the Curve.

So when you propose to move the `RotationMode` to `PathFollow3D` , I am actually agreeing with you. I also think the `artistic control` is not an intrinsic part of a `Curve3D`. So it is best defined and implemented on `PathFollow3D`.

> I looked at the code a little more closely. So, sample_baked_basis() doesn't make sense, what "basis" is it in Curve3D?

On the other hand, when you say this, I thought you imply that `rotation frame` is not meaningful on `Curve3D`, which I cannot agree, as the `rotation frame` is mathematically well defined on curve.

So now our consensus  is this: `rotation frame` on `Curve3D`, `artistic control` on `PathFollow3D`. Do I understand correctly?
author: xiongyaohua

body:
> I will call it rotation frame or frame.

"Frame" is not recommended because it conflicts too much with other terms in Godot. Considering the fact that `up_vector` is not called `B_vector` as well, it would be more appropriate to use the meaning by usage. TNB frame / moving frame is used for posture control, so I prefer to use the "posture". Or, it could use "rotation" just in this use case.

> So it is best defined and implemented on PathFollow3D.

The problem is that similar implementations have already been merged in `Curve2D`, so it will not be consistent. In `Curve2D`, `Curve2D::sample_baked_with_rotation` receives a value called "ahead", which is unrelated to `Curve2D`. If `sample_baked_with_rotation` is defined in `Curve3D`, it is not unnatural for `Curve3D` to have `enum RotationMode`.
author: TokageItLab

body:
> so I prefer to use the "posture". Or, it could use "rotation" just in this use case

Fair enough. Then I use `posture` in our discussion. For API I will keep using "rotation".

> Curve2D::sample_baked_with_rotation receives a value called "ahead", which is unrelated to Curve2D

This "ahead" parameter is not for `artistic control`. It is a hack added to patch non smooth loop, more like "Curve3D::loop_smoothing_enabled"(removed, following your suggestion). It is inherit from old implementation, and no longer necessary. I think I will propose to remove it in follow up PR. Then we will have symmetrical API for 2D/3D.

>  if you add a flag like posture_enabled to Curve3D, it would be possible to cache and sample basis with Vector<Basis>. This should allow for the correct implementation of sample_baked_basis()

Only the up vectors are cached is a conscious decision. In the initial baking implementation I actually cached the whole `posture` ,

https://github.com/xiongyaohua/godot/blob/17577571f6deee55387d6f775006342c1884311f/scene/resources/curve.h#L251-L253

Then I realized I don't need to. Because the up(N) vector is the most expensive to get, while the forward(T) and sideway(B) calculation is quite cheap (a vector minus for T, a cross product for B). 

So I decide to only cache up vector, and calculate the other two on the fly. This way we save 2 Vector3 (24 byte) per baked points(normally in hundreds or thousands).

body:
> help to prevent the model upside down in a case like a folded diamond shape?

I assume you mean the model roll 180 degree around the tangent in a very short distance at narrow corner on the curve? Then yes.

This is an intrinsic problem of the Frenet frame. Because at two side of the corner, the Tangent flipped, but Binormal didn't change, so the Normal(up vector) have to flip. See my drawing.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6020486/200214674-5ab5f750-eb4c-40cb-a481-00f2042f56d5.png)


So my implementation use another technique called [Transport Frame](https://gitea.yiem.net/QianMo/Real-Time-Rendering-4th-Bibliography-Collection/raw/branch/main/Chapter%201-24/[0374]%20[Game%20Programming%20Gems%202%202001]%20The%20Parallel%20Transport%20Frame.pdf), which guarantee the up vector change smoothly if the curve do not have sharp corner(z shape).

> Is this check necessary? 

I think yes. It checkes if the loop joint is smooth(tangents aligned at two ends).

Transport Frame introduce a new problem. For closed loop, the Frenet Frame guarantee the up vector well defined at the joint point, as long as the joint is smooth(the tangents of two ends align). The Transport Frame do not have this property, and the up vector will be different for the begin and end of the loop, which means a sudden change across the joint point.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6020486/200214752-1577be7d-6fea-415f-8edd-f0e4fee7e20b.png)

This  problem can be fixed by making the up vectors at the begin and end align, which require rolling up vectors gradually along the curve.  But if the joint is not smooth(tangent not aligned), no matter what you do the up vector cannot align. so I add this check, if the joint is not smooth, don't bother to fix it.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6020486/200214942-97bc7703-4a8c-4b62-ad7e-3d329903af44.png)

>  Also, this check prevents smoothing Depends on the value of bake_interval

I don't quite follow. Can you elaborate? I think this check depends on whether the joint is smooth (tangents at two ends of the curve align).
author: xiongyaohua
