body:
> created from the baked up_vector and unbaked forward_vector inside it

to not bake the forward_vector is just an optimization, because it is cheap to calculate on the fly. If performance is indeed an issue, baking cache for forward_vector can be add back easily.  

> since the only use of sample_baked_up_vector() is for paths in CSGShape

Another possibility is to remove `sample_baked_up_vector()` altogether, and let `CSGShape` use the rotation frame from `sample_baked_with_rotation()` directly. 

Currently the `CSGShape` path mode calculate its own rotation frame
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/324106b3dfd7a70c283f5adf17d53cfc48c8cdae/modules/csg/csg_shape.cpp#L1963
It use the same method as `sample_baked_with_rotation()` (`looking_at(tangent, up)`). So using rotation frame directly from `sample_baked_with_rotation()` is equivalent, but  have advantages for future: Let CSGShape path mode benefit from improvements on Curve3D for free, such as better tilt, bug fixes, performance optimization

body:
Code looks good, and it's definitely a welcome change.

Out of curiosity, I tried to bench this. Unfortunately, the bug report doesn't have any verifiable example so I made a simple test with a tool script and a for loop.

<details>
<summary>master version</summary>

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node


# Called when the node enters the scene tree for the first time.
func _ready():
	var start = Time.get_ticks_msec()
	
	for i in 100000:
		printerr("Hello %d" % [ i ])
	
	var end = Time.get_ticks_msec()
	
	await get_tree().process_frame
	await get_tree().process_frame
	print("-----")
	print("%d ms" % [ end - start ])
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>3.x version</summary>

```gdscript
tool
extends Node


# Called when the node enters the scene tree for the first time.
func _ready():
	var start = OS.get_ticks_msec()

	for i in 100000:
		printerr("Hello %d" % [ i ])

	var end = OS.get_ticks_msec()

	yield(get_tree(), "idle_frame")
	yield(get_tree(), "idle_frame")
	print("-----")
	print("%d ms" % [ end - start ])
```
</details>

The results are not impressive in `master`. Note, that we've already identified that the reworked editor log in 4.0 is very slow and inefficient due to RichTextLabel logic, and this needs fixing.

- With a `debug` build of the editor this test code runs for around `5.8s`, and with caching it takes `5.7s`.
- With a `release_debug` build caching performs worse (?!), `5.7s` vs `6.0s`. However, given the aforementioned issues with the editor log in general I can't be sure what slows the output panel down without some profiling. So let's pin it as a curiosity.

The results with the current `3.x` are more interesting. I've only tried `debug` builds, and the test code takes `2.4s` before the changes and `2.0s` after my crudely made backport. So there is a definite improvement, given the extreme amount of lines printed, this feels like a good percent (20%!).

To be completely fair we'd need to compare to a debug build of 3.4.5. But without a test project that the reporter can reproduce this is just a guessing game. Their use case may be totally different in details and can run into other issues. Without an MRP it's impossible to be confident that we fix the reported problem and not just _a_ problem.

-----

Either way, controls need to cache theme items. It's not a cheap operation to fetch them all the time, because many things need to be considered, and the tree needs to be partially traversed upwards. This is true even if we take the 3.4 version (or earlier).

So this is good.

There are no sign bits, and there is a 5-bit biased (15) exponent for each channel, 6-bit mantissa for R and G, and a 5-bit mantissa for B, as shown in the following illustration.

body:
> If so, the size of the space for drawing icons and text will be different from that in `Button::get_minimum_size`.

Well, drawing happens on the actual size, not on the minimum size. Button can expand beyond its minimum size and that shouldn't affect the drawing logic, so such a discrepancy should not lead to problems.

The problem is that the minimum size of a stylebox should be _at least_ equal to its margins. Which is why by default `StyleBox::get_minimum_size()` returns a sum of stylebox's margins, and a lot of GUI code just assumes that the method is a shorthand for getting all the margins combined. This is an incorrect assumption.

The minimum size can be changed for a particular stylebox implementation. And when you calculate the minimum size of the button, you should respect that and take the full `StyleBox::get_minimum_size()` into account. But when you're deciding on the drawing area, you should only offset it based on the margin values, and not on the min size. Perhaps it's worth adding a method to stylebox to return the combined value of margins, because we've already needed that in the recent Tree PR. But for now, you can simply explicitly make `get_margin` calls for each side and use that.

- If inside a thread, drop all messages that are not "core:" (which is the debugging part, or a list of "thread-safe" prefix)
- If inside main, process all messages regularly.
else:
- Process all messages from main (if main is blocked, and no thread is debugging, messages will simply queue up until main returns available or a thread reaches a breakpoint/error).

We could also then (in a separate PR) further tap into Thread/Mutex/Semaphore to poll_events from main at a regular basis in debug builds (like we do for infinite loops in scripts).

I went back and tested the behavior of *Main* when it is held in GDScript code, and yes it was a bug fix (not an enhancement.)   It just blocked on the "held threads" barrier and didn't process things, so remote inspection generally didn't work when debugging non-main threads (unless *Main* was idle.)

I implemented the change outlined above to let *Main* spin and process messages but nothing else, as soon as it executes in the script engine(s).  In a "normal" program, it will immediately enter this state when another thread is being step executed.   That fixes being able to remote inspect nodes while debugging other threads.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/compare/2b55d9f4b2ddc2b13d5977a09177f96390ab5908..217f9316f353f23c8517ef43a22374ce53469002
author: derammo

body:
As I also explained in the contributors chat, I think adding channels to the `RemoteDebuggerPeer` is an unnecessary complication, and it will actually introduce more issues than it solves.

First of all, it forces every `RemoteDebuggerPeer` implementation (tcp, websocket, etc) to implement channels.
This is an incredible overhead when it could be done (assuming separate queues are needed) by wrapping around "poll" so it routes messages to the appropriate queue and without requiring the lower level implementation to know this much about the debugger protocol (i.e. holding the queue in the RemoteDebugger, not the RemoteDebuggerPeer).

More importantly though, there seem to be this idea that we want "separate concurrent network streams" active in the engine debugger (in relation to https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4952 and SCTP, AMQP, or even using multiple TCP sockets).
This is not the case, there is one debugging session, and it is really important that messages are received in the order they are sent, introducing conccurent streams just makes things more confusing and error prone without solving any real issue.
There is no real reason to do flow control at the "wire level", because the "wire" is never stressed, the issues you are encountering are at the application level.

And this brings us to the topic of queueing messages that cannot be serviced by threads. Your main point about this was the need of dequeuing messages from threads themselves, because main could be held up by a join, mutex, etc.
But in that scenario main cannot service those queued messages anyway and they would simply pile up.
But at some point the queue will fill up and you'll have to discard messages anyway, and when it unlocks, the editor will also be swamped by replies to piled up messages.

So, in the end, discarding messages when main is locked that way, is simply inevitable.

To wrap this up:
- If we decide we really need separate queues, we should hold them, and route messages to the them in the `RemoteDebugger`, not the `RemoteDebuggerPeer` (but again, in the end, it will end up still causing problems in the scenario they are supposed to solve).
- Otherwise, and this is a simpler solution, we should just have threads only service while debugging and focused, and discard messages that are not thread safe.

In any case, we will need to be able to mark captures as thread-safe via a bool, so each capture (including user defined ones) can decide if it can handle being called by a thread or not.
Captures marked as thread safe will receive messages while being serviced by threads, while messages for non-thread-safe captures will be dropped when being serviced by a thread (or moved to the appropriate queue if we go that way).

They are both required, yes.

If you try to use `-march=` on x86 without the proper bitness or specifying `-m32`/`-m64` it will not work.

author: aaronfranke

body:
This makes it impossible for the user to use a custom `-march` value. For example, compiling with `scons optimize=custom ccflags='-O3 -march=x86-64-v3'` leads to compiler invocations such as `g++ -o core/core_bind.linuxbsd.editor.x86_64.o -c -std=gnu++17 -fno-exceptions -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -m64 -march=x86-64 [...]`, thus overriding the user-specified flag.

I'd suggest something like this instead:

```suggestion
    if env["arch"] == "x86_64":
        env.Prepend(CFLAGS=["-m64", "-march=x86-64"])
        env.Prepend(CXXFLAGS=["-m64", "-march=x86-64"])
        env.Prepend(LINKFLAGS=["-m64", "-march=x86-64"])
    elif env["arch"] == "x86_32":
        env.Prepend(CFLAGS=["-m32", "-march=i686"])
        env.Prepend(CXXFLAGS=["-m32", "-march=i686"])
        env.Prepend(LINKFLAGS=["-m32", "-march=i686"])
    elif env["arch"] == "arm64":
        env.Prepend(CFLAGS=["-march=armv8-a"])
        env.Prepend(CXXFLAGS=["-march=armv8-a"])
        env.Prepend(LINKFLAGS=["-march=armv8-a"])
    elif env["arch"] == "arm32":
        env.Prepend(CFLAGS=["-march=armv7-a"])
        env.Prepend(CXXFLAGS=["-march=armv7-a"])
        env.Prepend(LINKFLAGS=["-march=armv7-a"])
    elif env["arch"] == "rv64":
        # G = General-purpose extensions, C = Compression extension (very common).
        env.Prepend(CFLAGS=["-march=rv64gc"])
        env.Prepend(CXXFLAGS=["-march=rv64gc"])
        env.Prepend(LINKFLAGS=["-march=rv64gc"])
```

We need to set `CFLAGS` and `CXXFLAGS` individually, because `CCFLAGS` appear after `CFLAGS` and `CXXFLAGS` in the compiler invocation. Just replacing `env.Append` with `env.Prepend` would fix the example SCons command I gave earlier, but it wouldn't fix `scons optimize=custom cflags='-O3 -march=x86-64-v3' cxxflags='-O3 -march=x86-64-v3'`.

body:
@tinmanjuggernaut Probably if you have never use a subgizmo, you can't understand what it does. The subgizmo is a new feature implemented by @JFonS in Godot 4.0 that allows you to reuse the Node3DGizmo. For example, you can display gizmos on the vertices of a 3D object if you make plugin such as MeshEditorPlugin.

The Node3DEditor subgizmo system has virtual functions like `subgizmos_intersect_ray()` which are called by GUIInput, but you need to handle them independently in each EditorPlugin. For example, the selection behavior of Skeleton3DEditor must be implemented within Skeleton3DEditor. I called this process "notifications", but that is probably bad.

In Node3DEditor, when you select an object or empty space in the viewport, there is a behavior to select or deselect them, but this normal selection behavior gets in the way when using subgizmo.

For example, it is like that if you touch another object or empty space while in Blender's Edit mode, you will leave Edit mode and enter Object mode. That's not happening on the Blender, but to prevent this on Godot, the normal selection behavior of Node3DEditor must be bypassed.

If there are multiple EditorPlugin, `subgizmos_intersect_ray()`, `intersect_ray()` and other virtual functions will be called by all of them. At that point I worried about using the word "exclusive". So maybe I think such as `AFTER_GUI_INPUT_BYPASS_NODE3D_SELECTION` or `AFTER_GUI_INPUT_FOR_PLUGIN` are better name.

Even without subgizmo, that bypass behavior might be useful if there are cases where you want to put some kind of GUI around the object, but I don't have much idea about those cases.

body:
Just out of interest, why does the user need access to the underlying RID? Many Godot nodes use RIDs internally, but these are not generally exposed to the user, the user interacts using the client nodes and resources.

EDIT: Ah I see @DarkKilauea flagged this already.
Could this be a problem with the existing API if RIDs are needed for functionality? Where are they required?
author: lawnjelly

body:
This is a warning that if users use the NavigationServer API directly to change e.g. a navregion on a map or properties of the navregion then the NavigationRegion node will not show this changes cause it is displaying the cached values on the node. Maybe it could be worded different to make it more clear.

Half the NavigationServer API functions require RID's of the maps, regions, avoidance agents and depending on gameplay needs (e.g. multiple maps for actor sizes, procedural stuff, ai queries, ...) it can be a requirement to use the API to complement what is possible to do with SceneTree nodes alone.
author: smix8

body:
The question is not whether the warning is clear, but whether it is flagging a potential problem. In Godot the usual paradigm is as follows:

* Use nodes / resources - RIDs are hidden and not generally handled by users
* Use RIDs and servers directly - do not use the nodes / resources

The mix and match approach is problematic, for exactly these types of reasons, which is why it is avoided. This is why such warnings aren't written on all the nodes.

RIDs are essentially state machines operated by queue, and when you have two separate areas changing state independently it becomes much more difficult to prevent bugs. So the question is, what parts of the existing navigation system rely on a mix and match approach? Do we have to expose the RIDs _at all_ from the nodes?

For instance, if you want to pass a region (node or resource) to another node, it it better practice to pass the region, rather than the RID. The core engine will then be responsible for accessing the RID, and it is totally hidden from the user.

For instance using a `MeshInstance` you don't pass RIDs directly, you set a `Mesh` resource, which manages RIDs internally.
author: lawnjelly

body:
Approving this, but just to flag I'm not sure the whole policy of requiring users to be familiar with RIDs to use the navigation is good practice.

I'm not sure @akien-mga and @reduz opinions on this, but imo we should review the navigation and find out if these dependencies on RIDs can be removed. As I understand it, RIDs should be for advanced users only (due to the queue etc), beginners should not have to be exposed to them.

body:
Right now, parsers need to check the `parsed_geometry_type ` to know if they should be looking for collision shapes or visual meshes.

What if instead, we have two methods here:
- `_parse_geometry` (would parse visual geometry)
- `_parse_collision` (would parse only collision shapes)

Then, if a parser supports only visual meshes, it would implement `_parse_geometry`.  If it only supports collision shapes, it would implement `_parse_collision`.  If it supports both, it implements both.

This should simplify the implementation of parsers and might remove the need to pass in the target `NavigationMesh` at all.  The base parser would be in charge of calling the correct method based on the `parsed_geometry_type` field.

body:
a Python file can be parsed in two different cases with two different parsers:
- when executed by Python (Python parser)
- when typechecked by mypy (mypy parser)

`TYPE_CHECKING` variable is set to `True` when mypy parser is in use and the condition `if TYPE_CHECKING:` is really the recommended way to distinguish the parser. 
The condition can be used for various reasons, usually to avoid needles imports on runtime, or the imported resources might not be installed/present on runtime. In this case I use the condition to make sure the script will be unaffected by the new import even in case the file is used in some other scenario than via `SCons`.

Why is the import/annotation needed in first place (to answer your comment "I'm not really convinced yet by the usability of type hints in Python") below. Type annotations are by default opt-in, so in order to check what's going on in the function, it needs to be annotated even if the annotation itself seems useless. When annotated, it can catch various kind of errors (like #66659) without any manual testing required.

Anyway, thanks for merging it.

body:
The purpose is to force mypy to check the function. When a function does not have any signature, it's not checked (see example below). 

Yes, there's a config option to check even untyped methods, but that would mean to deal with ~80 existing errors in the codebase to have it running (I already checked), so start with opt-in checks feels like a good initial step.

```
$ cat check.py
def unchecked():
    1 + "2"

def checked() -> None:
    3 + "4"

$ mypy check.py
check.py:5: error: Unsupported operand types for + ("int" and "str")
        3 + "4"
            ^
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
```
author: yedpodtrzitko

body:

Those are not checks, though. Those are errors. And in this particular case I want to avoid throwing errors.

The problem this snippet solves is that buttons set text in their constructor. But at that point we don't have the cache yet. The cache is first set up on `NOTIFICATION_POSTINITIALIZE`. I didn't find a better way to do this for all controls as early as possible without manually running the method in each constructor, which would be quite awful. So for now, when `Button()` is constructed it calls `set_text` and hits these errors. Hence the extra check here. Didn't find any such issues with other controls.

It should shape correctly upon entering the tree anyway, so this check is only to silence the error from `text_paragraph.cpp`.

I looked into optimizing this a little bit as we are throwing away half the result of the matrix multiplication. Doing a little investigation I found that the compiler does optimize away a few instructions because the results are thrown out, but it still loads the entire matrix in SGPRs which results in a few extra memory operations and an increased SGPR usage. 

A potentially cheaper alternative is to just rely on z_near and z_far to linearize the depth as we do in the post processing effects. For example:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/d2a6a187f45345f00214c746924c57752a1f5260/servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/effects/copy.glsl#L244-L256

I got the above logic working on Vulkan, it is indeed much simpler. The `z_near` and `z_far` values are available from `scene_data`.

[The NDC's Z component differs between OpenGL and Vulkan.](https://johannesugb.github.io/gpu-programming/why-do-opengl-proj-matrices-fail-in-vulkan/)

I guess that's why this same logic returns wrong linear depth in case of the GLES3 backend. Fixing it.
author: viktor-ferenczi

body:
[Found this post useful](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11277501/how-to-recover-view-space-position-given-view-space-depth-value-and-ndc-xy/46118945#46118945)

The post agrees with the calculation quoted above and it indeed works on Vulkan, but not on GLES3.

`vertex.z = 2.0 * scene_data.z_near * scene_data.z_far / (scene_data.z_far + scene_data.z_near - (2.0 * gl_FragDepth - 1.0) * (scene_data.z_far - scene_data.z_near));`

On OpenGL 3 the carved out sphere is closer to the camera than it should be, so the calculated vertex Z value (view space) is wrong.

Pushed the code, so you can take a look. Thanks.

body:
Running a draw pass without motion vectors doesn't imply that the current offset is 0. 

The motion vector logic needs to run for all viewports that render motion vectors, but you could have a separate viewport that doesn't do MV. In that case, the viewport will run the non-motion vector branch, but it still needs to use the correct "current offset".

We could eventually add a branch that hard-codes 0 when none of the viewports render motion vectors, but we need to check if it actually makes a difference in performance, and whether the gain is worth the added complexity.

- [`try_get_path_from_dotnet_root`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/20e5237104ddd178f12bc501352e45a5e91e5048/src/native/corehost/fxr_resolver.cpp#L146-L158)

- [`get_dotnet_root_from_env`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/56095347ca1bacbc7a95e468f03f02ea808b9d9b/src/native/corehost/hostmisc/utils.cpp#L402-L426)

I would change this to “".tscn" files must work exactly the same as ".gd" files because they may contain built-in Scripts.” Here’s why:

1. The structure is more [parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelism_(grammar)).

The `Rect2i()` that gets passed into `viewport_attach_to_screen()` here is what eventually gets passed to `XRInterface::post_draw_viewport()` as the screen rect. body:
Well, the viewport is holding on to the window size, which is which is what's being passed into `XRInterface::post_draw_viewport()`. This would probably be easier to walk through on a video call where I could share my screen, but if you walk through the code backwards:

1. In [servers/rendering/renderer_viewport.cpp](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/b52305351d417c47ce019529fb511ecfd72c07e4/servers/rendering/renderer_viewport.cpp#L684) it has:
    ```
    Vector<BlitToScreen> blits = xr_interface->post_draw_viewport(vp->render_target, vp->viewport_to_screen_rect);
    ```
2. The `vp->viewport_to_screen_rect` above is set in [RendererViewport::viewport_attach_to_screen()](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/b52305351d417c47ce019529fb511ecfd72c07e4/servers/rendering/renderer_viewport.cpp#L875)
3. And it's `Window::_update_window_size()` which [normally calls `viewport_attach_to_screen()`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/b52305351d417c47ce019529fb511ecfd72c07e4/scene/main/window.cpp#L754). We don't want any of the other things that `Window::_update_window_size()` does normally, but when in XR mode, we still need the `viewport_attach_to_screen()` calls so that the code up in point nr 1 still works.

There's probably a better way to ensure that `viewport_attach_to_screen()` gets called when the underlying OS window gets resized than the way I did it, but I'm not sure what that would be.

The warning I was getting is [Scenario 2](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/reference/errors-and-warnings/nu5128#scenario-2). Since this package is a source generator it does not contain anything in `lib/` or `ref/` (only in `analyzers/`) because it's not a library and this warning is complaining that there's no assembly in `lib/` for the TFM `netstandard2.0` that we target.

So I think this situation is solved using this one of the solutions described in the documentation:

> If your package does not contain any `lib/` or `ref/` files and is not a meta-package, it likely does not have any dependencies that the package consumer needs. If you are packing with NuGet's MSBuild Pack target, you can set `<SuppressDependenciesWhenPacking>true</SuppressDependenciesWhenPacking>` in any `PropertyGroup` in your project file. If you are using a custom `nuspec` file, remove the `<dependencies>` element.

body:
I have reasons for changing this code:

1\. `_get_frame_duration()` moved below because it returns the duration of the current frame. It didn't matter as long as all frames were the same duration, but now without this change there is a bug that the duration of the previous frame is used.

2\. A limit on the number of iterations is needed to prevent freezes if, for some reason, `to_process` is each time much less than `remaining`. A similar protection is implemented here:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/44c55ad59b01dbf360777b1a9a18a229aeb1f4f7/scene/resources/texture.cpp#L2622-L2623

3\. In my opinion, my code looks more compact and clear (lines 178-211 -> 182-200).

4\. And a couple more points.

I respect your contribution to Godot and your experience (of course, much more than mine), but understand me: I spent more than 12 hours on this PR, so you can not reject any part without understanding why something was done the way it was. If you have more precise comments and suggestions for improving this code, I will be glad.

body:
Currently we only place these into the template, but they will not be added to the APK. When an AAR with an libopenxr_loader.so is added to the project, that will be included in the final APK. 

Unfortunately, due to the Android Gradle Plugin's limitation there is no safe way telling which .so should be added to the APK if multiple files with the same name are present during build. Here is an open issue about it in Google's tracker: https://issuetracker.google.com/issues/214395989

There are 2 options to solve this:
- Package the KHR loader that we build as a standard plugin that is included with the templates, so it can be easily added to the project. This is the option I would recommend.
- Hack the Gradle scripts e.g. to detect during the final copy that the OpenXR loader is missing from the APK and patch the APK.

I would support the first option is that a lot of Android projects are not AR/VR titles, so they don't need OpenXR anyways, and this way the APK will not include the additional ~500KB loader code.

What do you think?
author: kisg

body:
> It could be relevant for the editor, as we've had multiple issues/regressions over the years where tooltips would not properly use the editor theme. They should all be worked around by making it explicit in each case, but the bugs happened because we seemed to assume it would be automatic.

I actually have a solution in works for this, but it would probably wait for 4.1. But the basic idea is that instead of always falling back onto the "default + project" theme combo (even in the editor) we'd be able to define parts of the scene tree that fall back on an arbitrary combination of global themes. So in the editor all controls would fall back onto the "default + editor" theme combo.

This would help for the cases you describe, as well as all the times the project theme "leaked" into the editor, and will be helpful for some other UX stuff too.

I guess `strip_bbcode` should just remove all BBCodes without parsing them (even `[code]`). That is:

```gdscript
"[lb]text[rb]".strip_bbcode() # "text", not "[text]"
```

Otherwise, after `strip_bbcode`, we can get a string containing the BBCode, which even sounds wrong:

```gdscript
"[lb]b[rb]text[lb]/b[rb]".strip_bbcode() # "[b]text[/b]"
```

body:
Sorry for the delay, I think this goes in the correct direction, but it has few downsides.
One reason for having a single NetID was to avoid sending multiple (reliable) packets, one for the spawner and one for the synchronizer.
In short, synchronizers ID can be assigned in 2 ways, during spawn, or based on their path.
When assigning ID based on their path, an extra round-trip is required to confirm its ID, adding thus a brief delay before the first sync could be sent.
When synchronizers are assigned to a spawned "root node" instead, the replication system will reuse the NetID of the spawned object, avoiding the extra packet.

So, if we go change that part, I think we should still pack the synchronizer NetID in the spawn message (keeping the synchronization of spawned node "fast").
I think this could also be a chance to allow multiple synchronizers to control the same node (once we decouple the NetID from the object).

I will take a deeper look and get back to you ASAP (hopefully over the weekend).

body:
@Faless I started from https://github.com/godotengine/godot-cpp/blob/master/tools/targets.py but as I started syncing with the platform-specific `detect.py` I had to change some things which should likely be unified further in godot-cpp:

- Removed `0` to `3` flags as `3` isn't valid for MSVC, and IMO the use for these is limited. I think users can specify what they need with `CCFLAGS` if they need to override what we have (we could add `optimize=custom` for this if need be, to make sure we don't end up adding `-O0` from `optimize=none` after user-specified `CCFLAGS`).
- Removed `auto` as the logic is more complex than this, instead we handle it in `SConstruct` when handling the targets.
- Removed forcing debug symbols on `-dev` (ex `debug`) builds. There's a sane default now, but I think we should still give precedence to the `debug_symbols` option if specified.
- MSVC:
  * Removed `/Z7` for builds without debug symbols. Copy paste mistake I believe?
  * Added `/FS` for `debug_symbols=yes` as this was used in `platform/windows/detect.py`. Didn't assess what it is/does.
  * Removed `_DEBUG` as we weren't defining it before. I think it's meant to be set by MSVC when using `MTd` or `MDd` and IMO shouldn't be tied to `debug_symbols`, which is something we can strip (a `debug_symbols=yes` build stripped should be similar to a `debug_symbols=no` build IMO).
  * `size` optimization: the proper flag for this is `/O1`: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/reference/o1-o2-minimize-size-maximize-speed?view=msvc-170. `/Os` is a subset of `/O1` but the equivalent to GCC `-Os` is `/O1` as far as I know (this also makes a case for not exposing `0` - `3` flags as `-O1` and `/O1` are quite different).
  * Added `env.Append(LINKFLAGS=["/OPT:REF"])` which was in the Windows `detect.py`.
- GCC/Clang:
  * Added `speed-debug` for `-O2` on what used to be `release_debug` builds, as that's what we used there (apparently to keep potential backtraces somewhat usable).
author: akien-mga

body:
A couple differences for Android:

- `optimize=size` used to be `-Oz`, now it's `-Os` like for all other platforms. `-Oz` is apparently a more aggressive size optimization flag, but for the Web build we have this info:
```
# -Os reduces file size by around 5 MiB over -O3. -Oz only saves about
# 100 KiB over -Os, which does not justify the negative impact on
# run-time performance.
```

- `target=debug` used to force no optimization (`-O0`), now it uses debug optimization (`-Og`) like other platforms, which is a subset of `-O1` which does not hinder debugging.
author: akien-mga

body:
Some of these defines seem to be overkill for Android:
- `-fno-limit-debug-info` isn't defined on any other platform so not sure why it's needed here. Seems like it was added a long time ago by @RandomShaper in #6958, do you remember why?
- Undefining `NDEBUG` shouldn't be needed since we don't define it. But most importantly we want to avoid exceptions and AFAIK this controls exception behavior in `assert` so I'm not sure why we specifically want to re-enable it. Was also added in #6958.
- `_DEBUG` AFAIK is a MSVC specific define used for CRT debugging, so it makes no sense for Android. It's been there since Godot was open sourced, can likely be safely removed as it was likely an oversight.

body:
Looks good to me! 

For future reference, the reason this PR is correct is that it multiplies the base color of the sprite with the lights color in calculating the lights contribution before blending. In Godot 3.x lights were each rendered in a separate pass where you would redraw all sprites, calculate their color normally, multiply by the light, then blend using a fixed function blending mode. 

To achieve the equivalent in Godot 4.x we need to save the sprite's color and then multiply it by the light color for each light before blending.

body:
It shouldn't return `int` in the first place as [`double` can store integers out of the `int`'s range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-precision_floating-point_format#Precision_limitations_on_integer_values) (`int` isn't guaranteed to be 64-bit). It should return something like `int64_t` instead.

GDScript example (`4.0.beta1`):
```gdscript
var d = float(1 << 40)
print(d)
print(floor(d))
print(floori(d))
print(int(floor(d)))
```
Output:
```
1099511627776
1099511627776
-2147483648
1099511627776
```

body:
At a high-level, I think this is a great refactor! Working with WebSockets has always been a little awkward, mainly to do with getting the peer via `WebSocketClient.get_peer(1)` in order to actually send and receive packets. The first time I worked with it, I remember it taking me a little time to get my head around that.

I converted one real use of `WebSocketClient` to `WebSocketPeer` from this PR, and it was very straight-forward, except for figuring out how to handle a close request, which I think should be mentioned in the docs as I described in my other comments. There's one more real use of `WebSocketClient` that I want to try converting - I'll report back after, but I suspect it'll go fine as well :-)

Great work! :-)

State closing usually means we have sent a close request, but haven't received confirmation yet.
So, it isn't really safe to call `get_close_code` and `get_close_reason` here, but should be called when reaching `STATE_CLOSED`. I've clarified that in the docs.

body:
For example, if we do the following tween:
```
[1, 2] -> [2, 4, 2] -> [2, 1]
```
The result would be as follows:

When using MIN: ```[1, 2] -> [2, 4] -> [2, 1]```
When using MAX: ```[1, 2] -> [2, 4, 2] -> [2, 1, 0]```

If you use MIN, the final result may be smaller than the element in the middle of the tween, so someone may access out of bounds unless they know after the tween is over that it is smaller than the element in the middle of the tween. So it is safer to use MAX.

It's interesting that it doesn't do anything instead of inserting `5`.

X11 seems to define `XK_KP_Begin` as "BOL" which I suppose means "begin of line" as opposed to "EOL" which is "end of line": https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/proto/xorgproto/-/blob/25f3278b/include/X11/keysymdef.h#L182
 So I think they want it to be interpreted the same way as `Key::HOME` like `XK_KP_Begin`?

That being said, I'm on X11 / KDE and neither GTK+3 apps (Firefox) nor Qt5 ones (Dolphin, Konsole) seem to do anything with `XK_KP_Begin`. So I think the standard expectation should indeed be that this key doesn't do anything.
I'd suggest documenting it like this:

body:
We tend to follow the convention to use `e.g.` and `i.e.` without a comma after it:
```
$ rg "i\.e\. " -g'!thirdparty' -g'!*.po*' | wc -l
253
$ rg "i\.e\., " -g'!thirdparty' -g'!*.po*' | wc -l
17
$ rg "e\.g\. " -g'!thirdparty' -g'!*.po*' | wc -l
307
$ rg "e\.g\., " -g'!thirdparty' -g'!*.po*' | wc -l
6
```

So I would keep this as the convention here.

According to https://jakubmarian.com/comma-after-i-e-and-e-g/ `i.e.` without comma is British English while `i.e.,` with comma is the recommended American English style, but they point out that many Americans don't follow this style recommendation either.

No, this PR is simply not working. What you did there renamed the property only in the property list, but does not modify the `_get` and the `_set` functions setting those properties.

But this is a bad idea anyway, those properties are ordered in a table with the same amount of element as the number of custom data layers, and it is important that the TileSet's custom data layer count and the TileData custom data properties stay the same, and this is a lot easier to do with numbered properties than with named properties.

I don't know what gradle needs but I think it would be clearer if we followed the same structure as in scons, so:
```
supportedFlavors = ["editor", "template_debug", "template_release"]
supportedBuildTypes = ["regular", "dev"]  // In SCons it's just a boolean, so could be the same here if that works.
```

`dev_build=yes` can now be used with any target so `target=template_release dev_build=yes` is also a valid use case (gives `template_release.dev` lib). It's not a particularly _useful_ combination but it's IMO better if gradle follows the same logic of having only three targets and then a bool for `dev_build`.
author: akien-mga

body:
The new build model unfortunately doesn't match with Gradle's build layout.
Gradle has the concept of [build types and product flavors](https://developer.android.com/studio/build/build-variants):
- A product flavor is a different version of the project (e.g: demo version vs full version). This aligned somewhat better with the previous build architecture where `tools=no` corresponded to the `template` flavor and `tools=yes` corresponded to the `editor` flavor
- A build type on the other hand mapped to our previous concept of target and is used configure the build configuration (debug symbols, optimization, etc)

With the new build model, we still have two product flavors ('editor' and 'template') and still three build types ('dev', 'release_debug' and 'release'), so the gradle build model is still valid, we just need to update the mapping when we generate the scons command.
author: m4gr3d

body:
The build types are also shared across the project modules, while the flavors are linked:
- The `app` module maps to the `template` flavor
- The `editor` module maps to the `editor` flavor
- As a dependency, the `lib` module is configured to automatically update its flavor and build type to match.

> Good point, thought that is an issue already present with built-in type exports, I get that same behaviour if I export with type Camera2D, assign it then change the export type to something else like Sprite2D. I'd argue it could be done in another PR.

While that might work, it wouldn't fundamentally fix the problem. That would only update inline whatever objects are opened in the Inspector. You'd have to manually click on every erroneous node in the scene, re-save the scene, and then linearly move on to opening the next erroneous scene manually. It wouldn't globally and automatically update all of the project's scene files that have corrupted data integrity.

Whatever solution we use would likely involve a pre-existing mechanism for resources to recursively update in response to changes in their dependency hierarchy relative to other resources in the project. Something like... 1) save a Script, triggers notifications on all resources depending on that Script, 2) for each of those resources, they determine whether or not *they* need to update themselves. [sub_resource type="Resource" id="Resource_gw2eg"]
```Ini
resource_local_to_scene = true
script = ExtResource("1_khad7")
damage = 0
```

body:
In my opinion, the UID line does not need to be an annotation, since in this implementation the annotation features are not used (the argument is not validated, even duplication of the annotation is not checked). So the UID line could be implemented as a regular comment. The only benefit of an annotation is that it is documented and is a special syntax (custom annotations are not currently implemented).

If we still want to implement this as an annotation, then I think we should do the following:

1\. Add an exception for resolving and applying the annotation in the parser (for p.3), not in the analyzer. Just like it was done for `@icon` ([code 1](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/89cc635c0554cb2e518c830969ca4c5eedda0f4e/modules/gdscript/gdscript_parser.cpp#L520-L525), [code 2](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/89cc635c0554cb2e518c830969ca4c5eedda0f4e/modules/gdscript/gdscript_parser.cpp#L3837-L3853)).
2\. Add an validation: checking for duplication (as done for `@tool`, `@icon` and `@static_unload`, see [code](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/89cc635c0554cb2e518c830969ca4c5eedda0f4e/modules/gdscript/gdscript_parser.cpp#L3861-L3867)) and whether the assigned string matches the UID format.
3\. You can probably use the parser to read the UID instead of reading the file line by line. This will avoid incorrect detection of the UID annotation commented out as follow:
```gdscript
"""
@uid("uid_1")
"""
@uid("uid_2")
```
This is consistent with the fact that the parser (and not the analyzer) is also used to get the `class_name` (see #72444).
4\. Make sure that inserting a line with the uid annotation works correctly (that after inserting the line the script is reloaded, leading to re-parsing the source code).

As for the UID is stored in the script file, I'm worried that many people will be skeptical about it. But it's a core decision, I'm only talking about the implementation on the GDScript side and the choice between an annotation and a comment line.

body:
> There's an interesting comment on line 3173 about FPS reporting. Based on that, shouldn't this code be inside the IF from line 3173 (the if below)?

1% low FPS reporting is designed to be updated as often as possible, rather than just once per second. This makes the value less stable when you print out its value in `_process`, but it makes changes more reactive, which I think is better overall.

The editor performance monitor and `--print-fps` will still only update the displayed value once per second due to how they work (see the graph screenshot in OP).

In the long term, we could look into adding a smoothing algorithm like https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/63356, but I think this is better left for a future PR.

> Suggestion: Since it is already printing the FPS below (L3178 and 3181), WDYT aboud add the 1% low FPT there too?

body:
I'm using visual studio 2022 - 17.0.1 on windows 10

Let's assume it is indeed a problem with my personal setup. That put aside, let me then advocate in favor of increasing the buffer size.

The String::num function is meant to convert a double to a string representation. It allows specifying the number of decimal places, but it does not impose (explicitly or implicitly) a limit for the integer places of a real number. This double may be any double, even as large as DBL_MAX. If we let the buffer size be 256 as it currently is, even though very large doubles won't crash since we assume vcrt snprintf will truncate safely, the return value string will not represent the input value double. The user will expect a string with about 308 characters, but will get only 255. And since it is in fact an integer (since it is larger than 2^53), the returned value (as string) will represent a very different value from the input, wich will be several orders of magnitude greater.

body:
Previously `gui_is_dragging()` could be used, to query, if a dragging action is active in the current Viewport.

With the changes of this PR drag-and-drop becomes an operation that spans multiple Viewports, so now there are two concepts:
1. Is drag-and-drop active, that started in this Viewport? (This PRs `gui_is_dragging()`)
2. Is drag-and-drop active, that can drop in the current Viewport? (This PRs `gui_is_globally_dragging()`)

For the setting, that there is only a single Viewport in the scene, both behave identical.

After giving it more thought, I believe the second concept is more important for users, So I will update the PR and simply replace `gui_is_dragging()` by the second concept.

body:
Removed any modifications to `PackedScene` files. Added `GDScriptCache::clear_unreferenced_scenes()` that clears cached packed scenes if they are imported. The import check is done to prevent a "cyclic load" error from `ResourceLoader`.

The way "cyclic scene references" work is pretty simple. When GDScript asks for a scene with `preload()`, a empty scene is cached first, then is reloaded with the right path. So, if another `preload()` is called within the loading of the first scene, as the empty (and loading) scene is cached, it's possible to return its reference. See [modules/gdscript/gdscript_cache.cpp:357](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/67714/files#diff-a5502b90c5ce669d474f92292a3f2d6ef72ac9e1f1687534e3abce6b2640e703)

Unfortunately, I don't know how I could call `GDScriptCache::clear_unreferenced_scenes()` after the initial load.

body: That's a good question! I copied this code from the OpenXR plugin for Godot 3. I think there may have been a time before `OS::get_native_handle()` (the name of the function in Godot 3) was added to Godot, and this code was a fallback for if you used the plugin with an older version of Godot. We should probably just remove all those fallbacks, since we know we can rely on `DisplayServer::window_get_native_handle()`. And now that in Godot 4 we have multiple window support, it's more likely that calling `glXGetCurrentContext()` would give us the incorrect context anyway

The list of classes considered abstract by the Create New Node dialog should be a superset of the classes considered abstract by the code responsible for instantiating classes. Just as with the engine's own virtual classes, there are types that should be technically instantiable but still show up to the user as abstract.

Tested locally, it works as expected. Code looks good to me.

One potential UX concern is that the concept of *unit curve* isn't enforced in the inspector, so many nodes will expose the domain properties within the Curve resources even though they shouldn't. This adds visual noise to the inspector, but also room for accidental edits.

The best way to resolve this would be to add a new property hint similar to `PROPERTY_HINT_COLOR_NO_ALPHA`, except that `PROPERTY_HINT_RESOURCE_TYPE` is already used here to specify Curve as a valid resource type.

Nonetheless, I'll still approve this PR considering it improves Curve's usability for game design use cases, particularly for users who are not writing the scripts that handle the curves in question.

Or am I misunderstanding what you are saying?

body: Sounds good, although I'll still make the method return the exception instead of taking care of throwing. It's what I've seen in the .NET libraries, and it looks more readable to me. author: neikeq

body:
If the method always throws you can use the [`[DoesNotReturn]`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.codeanalysis.doesnotreturnattribute?view=net-6.0) attribute, but if we include the condition in the method then it doesn't always throw, so you have to assume that the method may return.

> It's what I've seen in the .NET libraries.

That's interesting, I made the suggestion thinking about [`ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty`](https://source.dot.net/#System.Private.CoreLib/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/ArgumentException.cs,108). This pattern allows to inline methods that call it[^1] although that doesn't apply in our case.

[^1]: Methods that throw are not inlined so by moving the throwing to a different method (e.g.: `ThrowIfNullOrEmpty`) the original method can be inlined.
author: raulsntos

body:
I didn't know there were public methods like that. The ones I saw are internal: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/57bfe474518ab5b7cfe6bf7424a79ce3af9d6657/src/libraries/System.Linq.Expressions/src/System/Linq/Expressions/Error.cs

I suppose it's not that consistent. In any case, I forgot the condition is now inside the method, so the argument about reachability doesn't make much sense. Now what worries me is the overhead if for some reason the compiler doesn't inline the call, although it should be smart enough to (specially if they have public APIs like that).
